speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: USE OF MACE CRAFTED AFTER FIRE OF 1916
speechtext:
With appropriate safeguards of the time set aside for proceedings pursuant to Standing Order 43 and following that for Oral Questions, I would like to indicate to the House two things.
Hon. members will notice at once that the mace in use today is not the mace which ordinarily rests on the table. The reason for that is a decision I made today to resume a tradition which was adhered to, if not initiated, by my very distinguished predecessor, Mr. Speaker Michener. The mace which is now on the table was crafted very quickly after the fire of 1916 so that parliament could continue to sit, the mace as well as the chamber having been destroyed in the fire 61 years ago today.
This mace was crafted so that the Parliament of Canada could sit elsewhere while this chamber was being restored, and that took some four years. During the tenure of Mr. Speaker Michener, this mace was used on the anniversary of that fire. It seemed to me to be a good idea to return to that practice, and so once a year it is hoped that the mace which was crafted for that purpose will be used and accepted by all hon. members on the anniversary of that fire as the symbol of authority, as it was used during those years when parliament had to sit off these premises.

subsubtopic: ADDRESS OF LOYALTY AND AFFECTION ON TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF SUCCESSION TO THRONE
speechtext:
I understand that there is a disposition, because of the great significance of the 6th day of this month, being the twenty-fifth anniversary of Her Majesty's succession to the throne, to proceed immediately with the motion standing under government notices of motions in the name of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and that motion reads as follows:
Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister), seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) moves:
That an humble Address be presented to Her Majesty the Queen in the following words:
To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty:
Most Gracious Sovereign:
We, Your Majesty's loyal and dutiful subjects, the House of Commons of Canada in Parliament assembled, beg to offer our sincere congratulations on the happy completion of the twenty-fifth year of Your reign.
The People of Canada have often been honoured to welcome Your Majesty and other members of the Royal Family to our land during Your reign and have witnessed directly Your inspiring example of devotion to duty and unselfish labour on behalf of the welfare of Your People in this country and in the other nations of the Commonwealth.
We trust that Your gracious and peaceful reign many continue for many years and that Divine Providence will preserve Your Majesty in health, in happiness and in the affectionate loyalty of Your People.
That the said Address be engrossed; and
That a Message be sent to the Senate informing their Honours that this House has adopted the said Address and requesting their Honours to unite with this House in the said Address by filling up the blanks with the words, "the Senate and".
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister stated, as reported at page 2634 of Hansard:
Mr. Pearson's guidelines, my own and those of this government, stated that if security information collected by police agencies in some way adversely affects the career of any person, that person should be entitled to refute the information, discuss it, contradict it and so on. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The House again in committee of the whole on Bill C-22, an act to amend the statute law relating to income tax. When the committee rose at the last sitting, clause 21 was under consideration.
On clause 21.

Mr. Chairman, at the last sitting I raised a question with the minister which is recorded at page 2571 of Hansard for January 31. I asked whether he had some information. The exact quote is as follows:
It is therefore important to know to what families this benefit is going according to size of family income. Does the minister have this kind of information for us?
I also entered a reservation; I pointed something out to the minister which all of us know, namely, that a lot of second income, especially in the middle and upper income groups, is earned on a part-time basis. Therefore, it is important to note the number of hours worked for the income in order to relate it to the sort of general family income, or know it by family income rather than by individual income. The minister invited me to look at the volume on taxation statistics, 1976 edition, which because of compilation relates to 1974, table 2. I took up the minister's invitation, as I always do. I always welcome the minister's advice on matters of this kind. As I anticipated, it is not possible to come up with an answer on child care expenses because it does not relate to family income. In addition, there are so many part-time incomes involved that it would not prove a point one way or another to use the statistics.
Looking at the table and making some comparisons, it is interesting how graphically it demonstrates the kind of argument we have been trying to make about the different kinds of tax benefits and who benefits from these taxation measures. There is the one that I described under child care expenses, where it is impossible to come to any firm conclusion on the

February 3, 1977
Income Tax A cl
basis of the evidence, the way that it is collected and compiled. In other areas it is possible to come to some conclusion. There are areas where it is quite obvious that the income tax system works with considerable fairness. They are not any of the measures presently before us.
I wish to illustrate the difference between how these measures are grossly unfair in comparison to other income tax deductions which have an element of fairness and relate to actual incomes and percentages that are going to people in various income categories. The one that jumps out is not really a deduction although it is called a deduction. It is a kind of tax credit because everyone gets it; it is a standard deduction. If we look at the table for the standard deduction, we find that the class of people with incomes to $5,000 who reported losses amounts to 38.4 per cent of the taxpayers in that group. Under the standard deduction that group receives 40.8 per cent of the benefits, which is quite fair.
In the $5,000 to $10,000 income class, which comprises 31.5 per cent of taxpayers, under standard deductions that group gets 32 per cent from the benefits. Again, that is fair in its relationship to the group of taxpayers. In the $10,000 to $15,000 income bracket, which comprises 18.7 per cent of the taxpayers, that group gets 18 per cent. In other words, the first three groups are virtually bang on. In the $15,000 to $20,000 of income class, which comprises 6.8 per cent of the taxpayers, that group receives 6 per cent of the benefits; again, a fair relationship to the size of the group and to the actual benefits they receive. In the $20,000 to $25,000 income class, which comprises 2.2 per cent of taxpayers, that group gets 1.7 per cent of the benefits, something less than the actual size of the group. In the $25,000 to $50,000 income class, which comprises 1.9 per cent of the taxpayers, they get 1.25 per cent of the benefits, somewhat less than the size of the group. In the $50,000 and over class, which comprises 0.4 per cent of taxpayers in Canada, under standard deductions they get 0.2 per cent of the benefits.
That is an example of a benefit in the income tax system which is roughly equivalent and fair virtually all the way through, give or take one or two percentage points on each side. This is really a kind of tax credit. I wish to compare that to something which is gross beyond belief when it comes to fairness. I am looking at the retirement savings plan premiums. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I would like to hand one of these sheets to the minister who will be here all afternoon. He may want to make a quick study of these figures to check their accuracy and make some comment on them. I have given the example of the standard deduction, stating that it is fair all the way through as it relates to the percentage of benefit going to a group, and the actual percentage as a group of taxpayers. We now look at the retirement savings plan premiums. Under the column of loss to $5,000, which represents 38.4 per cent of the taxpayers in Canada, the amount of the benefit this group gets is less than 1 per cent: the exact figure is 0.92 per cent.

This is exactly what we have been trying to say throughout the debate. This kind of benefit does not help people in the lower income categories because they have no income to offset RRSPs or else their incomes are so low that savings are minimal. They represent 38.4 per cent of the taxpayers and they get only 0.92 per cent of the benefits. In the income class from $5,000 to $10,000, representing 31.5 per cent of taxpayers, benefits received amount to 10.18 per cent. In the $10,000 to $15,000 income class, which represent 18.7 per cent, this group of taxpayers gets 20 per cent of the benefits, roughly equivalent to the size of the group.
It is interesting to find, as one looks through these examples, that this is the one group which is roughly in balance. This is true of the standard deduction, certainly, because everyone is in balance there. But with regard to virtually every program this group receives its percentage of the benefits. But the groups below get less and the groups above get far more. If we turn to the $15,000 to $20,000 income class, which represents 6.8 per cent of the taxpayers, we find they get 20.6 per cent of the benefits, three times as much as those in the $10,000 to $15,000 class, and an incalculable percentage as compared with those whose incomes are less than $5,000. Turning to the group getting between $25,000 and $50,000, representing 1.9 per cent of taxpayers, we find that this 1.9 per cent is getting 24.5 per cent of the total benefit. When we come to the income class receiving $50,000 and more, a class which represents 0.4 per cent of taxpayers, we see that this group gets 8.6 per cent of benefits, roughly 16 times what one would consider to be a fair percentage.
In our argument up to the present we have used tables to show that people at certain income levels get $200 in benefit, say, and that people at higher income levels get twice as much, and so on. But I do not believe anything shows the inequities so graphically as these tables. Some programs under the Income Tax Act are reasonably fair, but others are grossly unfair. The significant thing is this: the programs which are really out of proportion are the ones for which the minister is pushing hardest. Indeed, he has to bring in closure to ensure that they will take effect.
I should now like to give the committee some further examples. The interest income deduction provision tends to be reasonably fair and progressive. People with less than $5,000, representing 38.4 per cent of the taxpayers, receive 27.67 per cent of the benefits. That is not quite in line with their numbers in percentage terms, but it is much better than the 0.9 per cent they get under the retirement savings plan. Turn, now, to the group getting between $5,000 and $10,000. In interest income deductions they get 29.3 per cent, again roughly in line with their percentage as a group. If we go to the $10,000 to $15,000 income class we find they receive roughly 30 per cent of the benefits, which again is roughly in line. But even when we are talking about a reasonably progressive program, the moment we move to the group getting between $15,000 and $20,000 the figures begin to spread apart, because this group, representing 6.8 per cent, winds up with
February 3, 1977

10.4 per cent of the total benefit. The 2.2 per cent of taxpayers in the $20,000 to $25,000 group wind up with as much as 4.7 per cent, and in the $25,000 to $50,000 group, 1.9 per cent wind up with 5.5 per cent of the benefits. This is twice as much as its numerical percentage should entitle it to.
As for those with $50,000 or more, even under the terms of this interest income deduction which was brought in essentially to compensate for RRSPs, benefits from dividends, and so on, which the low income earners were not supposed to get, the 0.4 per cent of taxpayers receiving this high level of income still get 1.6 per cent of the benefits, four times as much as their numerical percentage would indicate they were entitled to, in our view. So even with respect to provisions which are supposed to redress the balance and make up for the benefits the rich are getting in other ways, the rich do not fare badly.
Let us turn, now, to consider the item "Other expenses of employment". This is an interesting example to take. I have given the figures with regard to the general expenses allowance which is $150 for everyone. But looking at the other items one finds the same "askewness" in terms of the number of taxpayers in certain groups and the benefits they receive. But those in the income class getting less than $5,000, representing 38.4 per cent, receive 1.93 per cent of the benefits from "Other expenses of employment".
I assure hon. members that if they go through these figures, they will find they are running roughly true at every level because this group is consistently getting the least benefit in relation to its percentage of the population. But as we move into the higher income ranges we find the picture changing. Those in the $20,000 to $25,000 class, which represents 2.2 per cent of the taxpayers, are getting 12 per cent of the benefits here. They are getting extra benefits because they are able to make deductions which the ordinary worker is unable to make.
If we go to those receiving between $25,000 and $50,000, representing 1.9 per cent of taxpayers, we find they are getting 19 per cent of the total benefits under this provision for other expenses of employment, while those receiving $50,000 and over, representing 0.4 per cent, are getting 6 per cent of all the benefits, some 15 times more than their percentage as taxpayers would seem to justify.
Even when it comes to medical claims it is still the rich who benefit most. One might ask why. Are the rich less healthy than the poor? One would think the opposite was the case. Do the rich suffer from some special, esoteric forms of sickness to which the poor are not subject, and do they, as a result, spend more on medical treatment? This does not appear likely to me, and I do not think experience would suggest it. Yet when we look at the medical claims we find that the group receiving less than $5,000, and representing 38.4 per cent of taxpayers, gets only 17.25 per cent of the benefit package. From $5,000 to $10,000 it is roughly equal. The position is the same from $10,000 to $15,000, but when we go from $15,000 to $20,000 the pattern emerges as before. While this category represents only 6.8 per cent of the taxpayers, these taxpayers are getting 10.7 pier cent of the benefits. Then when we move to the $20,000 to $25,000 income group, representing 2.2 per cent of
Income Tax Act
taxpayers, they receive 5.9 per cent of the benefits, I suggest double the benefits that their position in the tax structure indicates is fair. Those in the $25,000 to $50,000 category, representing 1.9 per cent of taxpayers, are receiving 8.1 per cent of the benefits in terms of medical claims that are deducted. The $50,000 and over group, representing 0.4 per cent of taxpayers, receive 4.5 per cent of the benefits, which is 20 times as much as the benefits that go to people in the lowest income category. That is the effect of these kinds of deductions.
The minister may say-I hope he will reply-that this is a characteristic of the progressive income tax system; that the more money you make, the more benefits you should receive. If that were so, the percentages should remain constant. It seems grossly unfair that one group of people should be collecting infinitely more by way of benefits under our tax system than any other group; really these kinds of deductions are subverting the progressiveness of the income tax system.
When you have made all these deductions, Mr. Chairman, and put in all these claims, the income tax system does not look all that steep anymore. I think this is a very graphic way of demonstrating the point that we are trying to make in this debate, which is that the government's approach to the problem is wrong. There are, in fact, ways to do this properly. I have already pointed out that allowances like the general expense allowance offer equal opportunity to people in all income groups, and this seems to me to be fair.
Why do you say that?
Because I think society is far better when that kind of fairness is perceived to exist in the taxation system.
That is egalitarianism. It is not worth the paper it is written on.

That is right, it is egalitarianism. I know that my hon. friend from Edmonton West does share my philosophy, but what I do not understand is how my distinguished friend can sit there listening to what I am saying and not take public exception to it by standing up and making a speech.
I intend to. I am just waiting for you to sit down.
Then I welcome that. That is what this place is all about.

speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I am obliged to the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge for having sent over

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
his table of figures. I think the interesting thing is that the table, far from proving his argument or stating the reason that he and his colleagues have for making the point they have for the last four or five hours, proves the very opposite. I do not want to distort the hon. gentleman's argument, but I will state it as I see it, and I am sure that if he feels that he should respond he may find time to do so.
The first thing that is rather interesting about this table is that while he has put in a series of comparative figures he has left out one very important series, very important in terms of retirement income. He has retirement savings plans premiums in the table, but not registered pension plan premiums. Who are we talking about when we speak of registered pension plan premiums? We are talking about the union worker, the blue collar or white collar worker, the man on the assembly line, the municipal clerk, the clerk in the federal public service, the school teacher, and so on.
The interesting thing about this-and these figures are on record in the earlier debate-is that with regard to retirement incomes the weight is heavily balanced in favour of those with incomes less than $15,000. Just as a quick estimate, something over 60 per cent of those with incomes of less than $15,000 make up this particular group. These figures have been left off this particular list, and if we are talking about registered retirement savings plans I think we should also take account of registered pension plans.
Let me take a look at the basis for his argument, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member says that he finds treatment of standard deductions equitable and fair and he has no quarrel with it. Let us compare it with child care expenses which he finds to be perverse in this respect.
So much of this results from part-time employment.

I suppose that if there is so much part-time employment one can argue that from both ends, the lower and the upper end of the income scale. However, for those who do report it, 25.7 per cent are claiming child care expenses among the income group up to $5,000; the standard deduction is claimed by 40.8 per cent of this group.
50	clearly in that first category of taxpayers there are more people taking advantage of the standard deduction in the lower income group than is the case with regard to child care expenses.
However, the situation is quite dramatic if you include those in the group earning up to $10,000 as well, which includes those with very marginal low incomes right up to those who are not really very well paid in the public service or in many private firms, particularly in small firms. You then find that
51	per cent of a group which comprises 31.5 per cent of taxpayers take advantage of the deduction for child care expenses.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, when you aggregate the two groups claiming child care expenses you see immediately that

77 per cent of a group representing about 70 per cent of taxpayers take advantage of this deduction. However, with regard to standard deductions, which the hon. gentleman found admirable, only 72 per cent of the same group were treated that way. So that on the basis of the figures presented by the hon. gentleman, if standard deductions are a fair and reasonable way of treating people, at least in those two lowest groups, then those drawing child care expenses are treated even more reasonably.
If we go to the other end of the spectrum, the hon. gentleman and his colleagues have been arguing that those at the upper end of the income scale have been getting a greater benefit, per group, than those at the lower end. With regard to child care expenses, for example, those earning between $20,000 and $25,000 a year, who represent 2.2 per cent of taxpayers, are getting 0.9 per cent of the benefit, and those earning between $25,000 and $50,000, representing 1.9 per cent of taxpayers, also get 0.9 per cent. Those earning $50,000 and over, representing 0.4 per cent of the taxpayers, account for 0.17 per cent of the total amount of deductions for child care expenses.
I am obliged to the hon. gentleman for his figures, but it seems to me that they show that the system, at least in regard to child care expenses, is not weighted in favour of the upper income scale earners, as is alleged by the hon. gentleman, but rather is most heavily weighted in favour of those at the lower end of the income scale, and more heavily weighted than standard deductions which the hon. member has just said are a reasonable way to deal with this particular situation.
The hon. gentleman obviously thinks that the taxation system is the principal method of providing income support. In this respect, of course, the government has proceeded to use other vehicles, such as the transfer payments under the family allowance program. In addition there is the guaranteed income supplement and old age security, and transfer payments through the Canada Assistance Plan in conjunction with the provinces. We have thus operated programs which make actual cash transfer payments to people at the lower end of the income scale.
With respect to the family allowance, it seems to me that the arguments being put forward in this debate contradict the ones we heard in the debate in 1972 and 1973, at which time the government put forward a measure which did weight that particular transfer payment in favour of those at the lower end of the income scale. As I recall it, the hon. member and his colleagues took the position that it should be across the board: whether your income is $5,000 or $50,000, you should be entitled to the same gross family allowance payment, although that payment would be subject to reduction for taxation reasons. At the time when we were a minority government this measure did not go through in the form we proposed, which would have favoured the lower income group more particularly, but as a government we favoured the transfer payments for those at the lower income level. Another good example is

AHOP, the mortgage interest assistance and other housing measures where literally hundreds of millions of dollars have gone into low income housing.
I may make one further comment. The hon. gentlemen thinks that this should be handled through the taxation system. The only extent to which I would agree with that is through the taxation system as an administrative vehicle for delivering the basic transfer payments referred to that we have put on the statute books and that Canadians are now receiving. It is really to determined whether the use of the taxation system as a transfer vehicle or an administrative vehicle for making those payments is feasible that we have that question currently under examination together with the Department of National Health and Welfare and other departments.
Going back to my first point, it is interesting range of figures which the hon. gentleman has given the House. It seems to me that they sustain rather forcefully the argument that child care expense reductions with which we are dealing here have favoured those at the lower end of the income scale rather than those at the upper end.

Mr. Chairman, I am very pleased that what is happening here today might well turn out to be a debate. I want to deal with some of the issues the minister has raised, and I am pleased he has raised them. One of the reasons I sent him the sheet was so he would not think 1 was pulling those figures out of the air, and I am quite happy to see him extrapolate some of the figures if he thinks they are to his advantage. However, I am sorry he overlooks the very important rider that I indicated about child care allowances, and neglects the other argument that makes the better case.
I was saying that we cannot really demonstrate anything from these figures about child care, but we can certainly demonstrate that the minister does not deny that, but I am rather surprised to hear the kind of argument he used on this occasion-because of the way the tax system is balanced, the deduction means far more to somebody with a higher income than to those on lower income. So there is no quarrel here and I want to leave it.
I want to say something else about family allowances. We have argued for a standard deduction. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre throughout the many brillant years he has graced this House, has argued for universality. I can remember how impressed I was when I was a little younger than I am now and I heard him speak on old age pensions. Someone asked him, "You mean, when we have a standard old age pension you will give it to E.P. Taylor as well?" The reply was, "Yes, the old age pension is a matter of right and it goes to everyone, to the poor and to E.P. Taylor. This is not a charitable act".
We have argued the same thing with regard to family allowances. We did not say, "Take it away from the rich." The rich have children, too, and they are entitled to some consideration. What we are saying is that they are not entitled to more consideration than the poor. We think E. P. Taylor is entitled to his old age pension so long as he hangs around Canada, and
Income Tax Act
if he has any children of eligible age, he is entitled to family allowance. We do not think people with higher incomes are entitled to more than the poor, because that is perverse and the kind of tax system we have is a very perverse system.
I hope the Minister of Finance clearly sees our point. We were not being unprogressive by voting against that measure and insisting that family allowances be equal for everyone. We were being consistent with the policy of this party over the years, that all people should be treated alike, especially under universal programs. Progressivity comes from having the income tax recoup whether it is the old age pension or the family allowance. That is what we are arguing about.
Let me deal with one other matter, since this is becoming a debate of sorts. The Minister of Finance said the income tax system is not the only way of distributing income. I agree with him that it is not the only way. One deals with every issue as it comes before the House, and one does not pretend it is the only way. There is a lot more that is wrong with the minister's party and his government than what appears in the income tax system. But today we are dealing with that system and we do not want to go over all these things.
The income tax system is a very useful way of redressing imbalances in other parts of the system, and I will give you the committee an example of this. When the Minister of Finance brought in the wage and price control policy with some reluctance, he did not use the words "rough justice"; they were used by the hon. member for Halifax. But I listened to the Minister of Finance on radio and television and found he had in fact picked up this phrase and called it "rough justice". It is at best rough justice. You cannot have an income policy that does anything more than control wages. The minister is beginning to realize that. Even when you want to control profits, there is an inherent difficulty in trying to do it in the kind of system under which we live. You cannot control dividends or prices effectively, but one thing the minister has been able to control-and this is one of the reasons the policy is so grossly unfair-is wages.
How do you get people to live with rough justice? The way to do is to say, "All right; we admit we have not been able to control much more than wages, but we will do something to the income tax system. We will see that some of the surplus income at least is siphoned off through the income tax system." But when the income tax system cannot do everything, as the minister says, it moves in a regressive direction and compounds the inequality of the wage and profit controls system. Then you have really accomplished the ultimate in injustice. This is why we have argued in favour of redressing the balance in the income tax system and at least making it progressive.
In the future we must have some kind of income policy, not the kind the government has now. The government will not be able to make it work through direct controls, because those controls only work very imperfectly and in some circumstances they cause a lot of problems. Therefore, you will have to use the income tax system to make up for the rough justice that occurs with direct controls. On that basis the minister should

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
recognize that while the income tax system cannot do everything, it should not at least make the situation worse in the way his proposals in Bill C-22 will do.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to rejoin the debate on the issue with the hon. gentleman, particularly on the question of transfer payments to individuals. He says that his party's dogma as stated by their high priest, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is that there have to be across the board universal programs. I was going to say it in the absence of the hon. gentleman, but I see him appearing spectre-like from behind the curtains. I would disagree categorically with the dogma of the party of the hon. gentleman regarding family allowance payments.
I was a supporter of the family income security program because when public resources of that kind are available, just like public resources in the housing program, the great weight of those public resources should be used to support those who have the least in our community and I think we should not have these across the board payments. Indeed, that has been the consistent policy in the case of retired people with the guaranteed income supplement program. I would not support a payment to E. P. Taylor, if he happened to be in this country, or to his sidekick, McDougald. I do not know whether he is here now.
Pay the old age pension.

Pay the old age pension: that is right, and this is the way it has evolved. As far as I am concerned, the weight of the pension system and the weight of the family allowance system should go to those who are least able to protect themselves in the economy. With the public resources which are available, that is the group which I, and I think many others in my party, would favour in dealing with these particular problems.
We are not really talking about the controls program but I will say just a couple of words with regard to the point the hon. member raised. Dividends have been controlled and profits have also been controlled. There have been rollbacks of profits in situations where they have amounted to excess revenue. One of the other factors-and this is observable from the aggregates of the economy-is that the profit level in Canadian firms has been below the trend level of the economy, and certainly below the level one would expect at this time. It seems to me we are almost getting to the ideal NDP state where nobody makes any money at all. Profit levels have been down. It is quite true that the controls on profits have not been as numerous as they have been with regard to incomes, principally because profit levels generally have been down.
The hon. gentleman was talking about this year of injustice to the wage earner. He talked about the difficulties wage earners had during 1976 because of the controls but, curiously, the working man has experienced a 4 per cent real increase in income through this period, principally as a result of the reduction in prices which was brought about by the controls

program. The controls have put more real income into the pockets of wage earners of this country and have had the very opposite effect to what the hon. member has suggested.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps we could come back to clause 21, and I will recognize the hon. member for Edmonton West.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge has been talking about rough justice. I wish he would at least be roughly relevant to clause 21. It seems that on any clause one can raise any subject which is within the four corners of the Income Tax Act, and it does not matter; but those who want to make a relevant contribution-and there are many in this House- find that with a limited time debate they are cut short. All I want to say about the comments with regard to the increase in child care expenses and the statistics we have heard ad nauseam is that the hon. member made one great oversimplification. He failed to point out the number of taxpayers who are spouses and therefore file separate income tax returns. I am sure the hon. member's observations would have been far different if he had considered family income.
It is all right to say a man earns $25,000 a year, but what if his wife is not working? The hon. member made some observations about the extraordinary, outrageous and disporportionate benefits a man earning $25,000 or $30,000 a year gets. However, if his wife is not working, he is the family breadwinner. Let us consider the man who makes $15,000 and whose wife works and makes $10,000. They are two separate taxpayers, albeit at lower levels. For a family earning $25,000, in which the wife is not working, there is no child care expense allowance. Where the husband earns $15,000 and the wife earns $10,000, there is a child care allowance.
I suggest that the table put forward by the hon. member fails to recognize one fundamental feature. As a matter of fact, even the minister in his observations on this fails to see that today there are hundreds of thousands of taxpayers who are married women and have to be classified as single taxpayers. They may claim the allowance for some of the children in the family. This varies. Each spouse picks the best advantage he or she may have under the Income Tax Act. It is a matter of sorting out the children and deciding who should claim the allowances.
The hon. member, however, lumps everybody into the same bag as though each taxpayer is the sole earner in the family group. It is the family group that we have to consider. Do not tell me that there is injustice to somebody earning $16,000 or $18,000 a year as a teacher who has a wife working part time either in an office, as a secretary in a school board office, in a school office, or in a supermarket, whatever the job may be, who earns, say, $6,000 a year. The hon. member has failed to take into account that there are two taxpayers in that family. I have a son who goes to university. He works part time during the summer. He is classified a taxpayer even though he may earn only between $4,000 and $5,000 a year. Therefore, all these suggestions with regard to the benefit of child care to taxpayers in this particular class are very misleading and
February 3, 1977

constitute an oversimplification. I find it extraordinary that the hon. member should have fallen into that trap. Frankly, it is an unconscious-I do not think he has done it consciously- misleading of the House for him to cite statistics such as those.
If the hon. member had been talking about 20 or 25 years ago when relatively few married women were working, perhaps his conclusions would have been more apposite, but today that is not the case and I hope that somewhere along the line in considering income tax we will get to the situation where joint income tax returns can be filed by a family group, husband and wife. It would be much more fair.
Hear, hear!

Then the hon. member could start making complaints with regard to the benefits of increasing the child care allowance from $2,000 to $4,000 as a maximum. Frankly, I was surprised. I think he has been misled by some of his research staff in arriving at his conclusion. He should study table 17 as it appears on page 160 of "Taxation Statistics 1975" which is headed "Returns with child care expense claims". He would find that the maximum number who claimed for the taxation year 1974 were in the $5,000 to $6,000 taxable group. I will put it on the record. For working mothers in the income bracket less than $2,800 there were 9,606 claimants; $2,800 to $3,000, 4,107; $3,000 to $4,000, 21,130; $4,000 to $5,000, 26,461; $5,000 to $6,000, 29,683; $6,000 to $7,000, 22,589; $7,000 to $8,000, 16,953; $8,000 to $9,000, 12,688; $9,000 to $10,000, 6,908; $10,000 to $11,000, 3,373; $11,000 to $12,000, 2,625; $12,000 to $15,000, 3,592; $15,000 to $20,000, 1,564; $20,000 to $25,000, 427; and, over $25,000, 412 claimants.
If the hon. member looks further at table 17, he will see the number of claims by working mothers and the number by fathers. A study of the statistics indicates that the tabulations and computations he made in assessing what class of taxpayer was receiving the benefit of child care expenses and registered retirement savings plans are totally wrong. He failed to look at the joint family income, which is where the real benefit lies. In the $20,000 taxable income class, which means a salary of about $25,000 with the normal number of exemptions, the chances are that the wife would not be working. As the income scale goes up, usually the wife does not work. Today the working spouse is a social phenomenon more than an economic necessity.
Oh, oh!

There are a number of cases where the wife does have to work to help maintain the home, but there are far more cases where couples have bought a house at $18,000 or $20,000 more than they would if she were not working, or bought a second car or wanted to do extra things. In such cases, the spouse works in order to justify a higher standard of living, not from economic necessity. There is no criticism of that; it is a social phenomenon of
Income Tax Act
today. Husbands and wives have decided to work in part in order to raise their standard of living, not to subsist.
Go down to Newfoundland. Tell that to your colleagues from Newfoundland.
In this city of Ottawa, in this very building, in Sudbury, in Sault Ste. Marie among the steel and nickel plants, there are many men earning very good salaries.
Come off it.
There are women who are also working in order to increase their standard of living.
They are all lawyers.
The hon. member should get his head out of that bag of doctrinaire prejudice he has because he is a member of that party.
Hear, hear!

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, is the hon. member for Edmonton West suggesting he is against those families in the Sudbury basin who are trying to exist and subsist within a regressive income tax structure by the wives having to go out to work? I want to know that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. This, surely, is not a point of order. The hon. member is making an argument. If he wants to ask a question, he should ask the permission of the hon. member.
If the hon. member is trying to suggest that people in Sudbury are generally in that category, then he is full of tripe.
Except the lawyers.

I will come back and look at the average income reported by taxpayers by district, and we will see where Sudbury is. It is certainly in the lower part of the table.
Mr. Chairman, I have here a letter from a man who says he is a teacher and whose wife is not working. He wonders about the increase in the child care benefits to $4,000 a year. I do not declare this a correct argument, but it is a point of view held by a number of people. It may be that hon. members will want to correct this, but at least we will discuss it. He writes:
There are many people who utilize the daycare-babysitting-deductions so that both parents can work, not in order to survive, but rather only to have a higher standard of living. Should parents whose combined incomes are in the $15,000 and sometimes much above brackets, i.e. $30,000 plus, be able to take advantage of tax deductions which were really aimed at the lower income sections of the community?
I am sure the hon. member for Nickel Belt would say that above a certain income there should be absolutely no allowance for child care. The writer makes this point:

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
Daycare expenses should be available only for those who are (a) single parents with pre-schoolers, or (b) parents whose combined incomes are below a certain level.
The writer feels that more women should stay at home and look after the children, because as a teacher he sees children who have been brought up by day care centres, not through necessity as in the case of the single parent of whom there are a great number. He feels that more children should be looked after at home by the mother, because as a teacher he sees what he considers to be almost social monsters as a result of lack of parental care. They are pushed out in the morning or dropped off at school or picked up by the bus, they lunch at school, drop in on a neighbour after school, and return home about the same time as the parents. That is the extent of their upbringing.
I want to put it on record to indicate that not everyone is in favour of, shall we say, this unrestricted subsidy to child care centres, for that is what it is. Personally, I feel that there is a need for child care centres to serve, particularly, single parents. Indeed, I would much rather the state provided that service for those people. It could be provided through provincial governments or municipal administration and for those whose incomes fall below a certain level there would be no charge. But beyond that fees ought to be charged and such centres ought to be considered as private schools and the double family income ought to bear the brunt of that charge. It ought not to qualify for the allowance.
Since the government has allowed inflation to go along unchecked for a number of years, certainly since the induction some years ago of the child care expense allowance, the ceiling certainly should be raised to the extent envisaged in the bill at this time.

Mr. Chairman, it is the first time I have the opportunity to rise on this issue and I would be happy if the minister could go back to his seat, because I would like to ask him a single question. After all I have heard since the beginning of the discussion, and I did not miss much, the longer the discussion of clause 21 goes on the less we understand. Every spokesman for the New Democratic Party tried to give evidence that clause 21 was for people with high income at the expense of those at the lower end of the income scale, whereas the minister is trying to explain that it is not true.
Yet, a while ago, listening to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) reading his letter, I was thinking that this letter says a lot. We were wondering what low income people could get from that, compared to people with high income. I think light always comes from the working classes, it is quite clear now.
I will ask the minister, who is getting advice from experts, whether he can tell the House what a couple, whether both are working outside or not, will get in terms of family income. From what the hon. member for Edmonton-Centre has just

told us, it is unfair that a spouse who works to raise a family and earns $25,000 and whose child is placed in a day care center should be disadvantaged in comparison with another couple in the same conditions but with an annual income of $50,000. I would like to know what each of these two couples is getting? If the minister is prepared to answer now, I will have only one other point to deal with.
That may be rather difficult to answer without knowing what tax rate applies or what deductions the individual is entitled to. But perhaps we can try to figure it out quickly.
Both are in the same economic situation.
You spoke of a couple earning $25,000, and another earning $50,000.
Yes, both are in similar economic circumstances, benefitting from the same exemptions, to which the same tax rate applies.

Their economic situation is not the same. One gets twice as much as the other. They may be subject to the same maximun deductions according to the bill, but the effect on their income tax will in fact be different. The percentage may be the same, but there will be a higher absolute amount where the income is greater.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. That is precisely what I wanted to hear the minister say. That is precisely because the error lies in the rate. A deduction is made in terms of the percentage of the tax paid. I can understand the hon. members of the NDP who fight for that principle, because I feel that if we want to be fair to those who have to entrust a child to someone's care, we should fix a set amount. For instance, we should say that $40 or $45 a week will be allowed, which amount could decrease as salaries go up, because whoever earns $25,000 cannot afford to pay as much as the person who earns $50,000. As a result, those who earn $50,000, under the system I am advocating, would not be entitled to deductions for child care while those who earn $25,000 or $15,000 would be allowed more deductions. That is what we should do if we want to help the couples earning whereas the minister indicates vaguely that he wants to give more help to the couple whose income is highest. In this case, the NDP are right.
No.

The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) says no. Of course, because the minister has already said that whoever pays more income tax should have higher deductions. That goes without saying. If you stick to the deduction by the percentage, it is obvious he will get more. But you must not forget that the one earning $50,000 who places his child in a day care centre will not pay more than the one with a $15,000 income. You have to be fair. Will the day care centre charge $150 a week to the one earning
February 3, 1977

$50,000 and $25 to the other earning $25,000? Come on, this is done only in senior citizens homes in the province of Quebec. In these homes, one person with a little more money will be charged more, but we must not get in the same mess. I may be wrong but if we want to give direct assistance to minimum income couples, I think the percentage ought to be forgotten. I would like the minister to say what he thinks about it.

Truthfully, to answer the hon. member's previous question, the taxpayer earning $25,000 will have a marginal tax rate of 39 per cent, and if he deducts the $4,000 maximum indicated on the bill, he would then get $1,560. However on a taxable income of $50,000 the marginal rate will be 43 per cent and the tax saving will amount to $1,720. But I must point out that the total federal tax for the taxpayer will be $7,250 if he earns $25,000, while it will reach $17,440 for the one who earns $50,000 and in that sense the tax paid by the latter is quite higher than that paid by the first taxpayer.

I realize once again that it is quite fine. I am told that the taxpayer who earns $25,000 will have a reduction of $1,560 in comparison with $1,720. Still the higher wage earner will receive $160 more than the lower wage earner.
He pays more.

Well, he paid more because he had more money, but if we consider the needs of the couple we must take an entirely new position. Let us consider the one who paid and not the needy. In that case it is somewhat like the case of pension plans, we agree on that point. A man needs an adequate income if he is to invest. The investor must be rewarded, because investments are needed. Such is the line of reasoning.
But with regard to child care expenses, it is very difficult to take. The hon. member for Winnipeg can say no all he likes, it is very difficult to take when one wants to plead for the family...
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) on a point of order.

I hope the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) will admit that Winnipeg is not Edmonton. I come from Edmonton! I want to make a slight correction. Edmonton is not in greater Winnipeg, it is further west. Edmonton is a lot more important than Winnipeg!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member's point is well taken.
Income Tax Act

A few more figures. Calculations are continuing. I provided the tax figures on an income of $25,000, which is $7,250, representing 21 per cent. But for a couple with an income of $50,000 the amount would be $17,440 and this deduction represents 9.8 per cent of their income tax.

Mr. Chairman, I understand very well what you have just told the House but I maintain my position because it so happens that the tax deduction applies to the amount of tax paid; this is all very well, but I recognize that we had better do it otherwise if we really wanted to help directly the needy family.

Mr. Chairman, the debate this afternoon has been an interesting one, with interventions from the minister and my friend from Edmonton West. We have been talking about clause 21 of Bill C-22, the child care deduction allowance. Throughout the discussion we have been ranging over the concept of whether this is a deduction that benefits upper income Canadians more than lower income Canadians.
The Minister of Finance has been trotting out the income tax rate and how the rate increases as we go up the income ladder. He has been making the argument that indeed we have a progressive income tax system, that upper income Canadians pay more in taxes, and therefore the kind of complaints being made by the NDP about these deductions really do not hold much water. He states that upper income Canadians pay more income taxes, and therefore they should be entitled to the benefits of these deductions. I wish to address myself to that point and to the whole concept of what makes an income tax system fair. To make an income tax system fair, we have to base it on the principle of the ability to pay, namely, that the more one earns, the more one is able to afford to pay higher taxes. The fact that with our income tax system the percentage tax rate is lower for people at the low income level, and higher for higher income people, indicates that the government believes in the concept of progressivity: the more one makes, the more one is able to pay.
What we have been complaining about with regard to Bill C-22 is that that principle is undermined by virtue of deductions that are in the bill. What these various deductions do is reduce the taxable income of a person, and hence the rate at which that tax will come into effect. I would like to show how this happens by zeroing in on the clause before us, the child care deduction. The bill will double the deduction from $500 per child to $1,000 and bring the family maximum up from $2,000 to $4,000. In 1974, the last year for which we have up to date statistics, the child care provision under the old rate cost the government over $29 million in taxes that would otherwise have been collected if that deduction had not been available. It is interesting to note that this was only $3 million less than was spent by all levels of government in directly subsidized day care programs.

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
I hope it will be seen by the conclusion of my speech that there are better ways of spending this money than by the present deduction system. We in the New Democratic Party do not object to the idea of a child care deduction. We know that it is becoming more and more expensive to raise a family in this day and age of increasing costs, and that the burden falls harder on low income Canadians. We agree there should be some compensation for raising children, in terms of the income tax system. However, we ask the government and the public to examine how this present deduction system works and whether it is a fair way of providing support for families who are raising children. In other words, who does it help the most: the lower income families who obviously need aid, or upper income Canadians who are better able to meet ever-increasing costs?
We contend that it is the well-off who benefit most from these deductions. The Minister of Finance and spokesmen for the Conservative party say this may be true, but since we have a progressive tax system the well-off pay more tax anyway and for this reason the programs are not unfair. In response to that argument I should like to quote from a current study which was undertaken recently by a government-funded agency, the National Council of Welfare. I quote from page 20 of a council report entitled "The Hidden Welfare System." The authors considered the child care deduction system and say:
When the child care deduction, or, for that matter, any deduction or exemption, is examined in the light of the progressive tax rates, it become obvious that it stands the ability to pay principle precisely on its head. A deduction always gives a greater benefit to persons with a higher income and a lesser benefit to persons with low incomes. This is because deductions always take money out of a person's highest tax bracket-the bracket which is taxed at the highest rate applicable to his income.
We are not, of course, against child care allowance. But the system should be structured in such a way that deductions in respect to it do not subvert the concept of progessivity and ability to pay. Let us see how the present system works and how the bill before us will work when passed. Take the example of two women, one a minimum wage-earner earning $6,000 a year. Consulting the 1976 tax schedule, we find that if she were allowed no child care deduction, federal and provincial tax upon that $6,000 would amount to $518. But if she is allowed the child care deduction in respect of one child, her taxable income is reduced by $1,000. Therefore, federal and provincial tax would be reduced to $261 and the child care deduction would provide a tax saving of $257.
Now take the case of a woman earning $20,000. Her taxes on this amount, before the child care deduction, total $4,972. If she takes advantage of the child care deduction, her taxable income is reduced by $1,000, which in turn reduces her tax bill to $4,592. Her tax saving amounts to $380. In other words, each woman gets the same basic deduction of $1,000, but the tax saving in dollar terms is quite different. The low-income person saves $257, but the upper-income person saves $380. So what we must concentrate upon is the dollar effect of the reductions built into the tax system.

What the income tax system should be doing is narrowing the gap between the rich and the poor to provide relief for those living below the poverty line. It is shocking to note that in this wealthy country there are five million Canadians living below the poverty line. The Prime Minister himself stated that it was a goal of his government to narrow the gap between the rich and the poor. I note that the Prime Minister said in 1971:
The whole idea of redistributing wealth so that there might be a greater opportunity for all has been a national goal of this government.
That was in 1971. But what has happened since is that successive budgets by various finance ministers have failed to achieve this goal. Wealth has not been redistributed and the gap between the rich and the poor has not been narrowed. I should like to give some figures to indicate how the tax system has become perverse. In 1951, the bottom 20 per cent of income earners got 4.4 per cent of the total national income. Twenty years later, in 1971, the same bottom 20 per cent found their percentage of the national income reduced; they received only 3.6 per cent. In 1975 they registered a fractional increase which brought them up to 3.9 per cent.
Consider what has been happening to the top 20 per cent of income earners. Their share of the income pie has grown. In 1951 they got 42.8 per cent of the total national income. In 1971, the year in which the Prime Minister disclosed his goal and spoke about narrowing the gap, the same 20 per cent increased its share of the total national income and got 43.3 per cent. In 1975 that figure was reduced only marginally to 42.4 per cent. So through two decades each group finds itself in relatively the same position. There have been marginal movements but the gap was just as wide as it was. This is what we object to so strongly in the bill before us. The deductions here will perpetuate the inequity in the economic system as it pertains to low income earners. Moreover, the national government is losing billions of dollars of potential tax revenue, revenue which might be used to introduce income support programs in favour of lower income Canadians.
That would sure create a lot of jobs, too.

The National Council of Welfare estimates that all these various provisions cost the treasury $4.6 billion in lost tax revenues in 1974, and goes on to say that if the government were to eliminate or revise only half of these provisions, the tax revenue available to the federal treasury could be used to eliminate poverty for the five million Canadians living below the poverty line.
What we would like to see, instead of the present provision in clause 21 of a standard $1,000 deduction applied to both low income earners and upper income earners, is a new system of tax credits which would provide some kind of relief to families who are raising children. It would be arranged in such a way as not to benefit upper income Canadians more than lower income Canadians. Again I quote from the National Council of Welfare report at page 21. This is their finding:
February 3, 1977

The way to eliminate this inequity is to replace the child care deduction with a child care credit. (A tax credit is just what its name would imply: a credit of a fixed amount which each taxpayer could apply against his/her tax bill-or, in other words, a fixed amount of tax which he/she does not have to pay.)
In the example above, suppose the child care deduction were eliminated and replaced by a tax credit of $350 per child. The two women-
They are the two women I mentioned earlier in my speech.
-Would both then be eligible for the same $350 credit. For the woman whose earned income was $6,000, this would mean a $93 reduction in her tax bill. (Instead of the $257 tax saving she now receives from the deduction, she would have her taxed reduced by $350, a difference of $93.) The $20,000 a year woman would have her tax bill increase by $30 (since the present tax deduction gives her a saving of $380, but the credit would only give her a saving of $350).
So 1 submit that there is a way through the tax system to help families that are rearing children. The way to help them is not, as this bill proposes, by means of a standard deduction but, rather, a tax credit. Then those who need help the most- that is to say, those at the lower end of the income scale- would receive the maximum benefit, rather than, as the system is now, those at the upper end of the income scale who do not need the kind of tax saving offered as much as those at the lower end of the income scale getting the unfair advantage which is inherent in this provision of the bill.
As a Canadian, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about fairness in our tax system, and the more I look at the tax system that is designed by the Liberal government, supported by their Conservative friends, the more I see how it discriminates against those who are least able to fight back in terms of their income and their political strength. That is why we say the bill is unfair, that there are better ways to provide assistance to families. The better way is the tax credit, not the regressive kind of deduction that the government is proposing in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, may I just add a postscript to that. According to the figures presented by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, 77 per cent of the benefits from child care expenses go to those with incomes of $10,000 or less.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance loves to point out in percentage form who receives the benefits. I do not quarrel with the concept that lower and middle income Canadians should receive benefits from the child care deduction system. But what I do quarrel about is the fact that upper income Canadians, who really do not need the kinds of deductions that we have here, are benefiting in dollar terms more than lower income Canadians. Therefore, if the minister is concerned about fairness and not with just quoting percentages showing who gets what, he will remove this provision from the bill and replace it with a tax credit system.

Just to respond to the hon. gentleman, he was making the argument that it was politically expedient for us, for some reason, to put in a measure favouring those in the upper income group. In fact, it favours the lower income group, so it seems to me that the hon. member's argument does not follow.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, when you look at the total number of provisions in our income tax system of which the minister is so proud, since the minister is so fond of talking about averages, if we add up all the exemptions and deductions permitted in the income tax system we find that taxpayers earning $5,000 average a tax saving of $244, whereas taxpayers earning over $50,000 save about $4,000. I would ask the minister, what is fair about a tax system which permits 27 per cent of all tax savings to go to the top 5 per cent of tax filers, while only 33 per cent is distributed among the 70 per cent or more of lower or middle income? I say that is not fair.

With a progressive income tax system, Mr. Chairman, people at the upper end of the income scale pay a much higher dollar amount, if the hon. member wants to talk in terms of dollar amounts. What I am pointing out is that from the figures that his colleague tendered to the House it appears that the vast majority of taxpayers in this country who take advantage of child care expenses, which is the clause we are dealing with at the moment, earn incomes under $10,000. So it is scarcely a measure that is weighted in favour of the upper income group.

Mr. Chairman, I never cease to be amazed to find, when we are discussing bills having to do with income tax, a close liaison existing between the Liberal and Conservative parties. They certainly form a coallition to support this kind of maldistribution of income tax. The point that my colleague for Sault Ste. Marie was making seems to me a very legitimate one.
He never made one, though he tried to.

We are not objecting to child care expenses being increased. What we are saying, in effect, is that because it is a progressive tax system this is another distortion in the system. As we go through the bill we see other give-aways and exemptions are permitted only for people who are earning large amounts of money, and therefore it becomes a distortion when it is superimposed upon-
What is your salary?
Well, you do the same job as I do, so you know my salary.
If I did my job like he does his, I would not want it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the debate on Bill C-1001, an act to incorporate Continental Bank of Canada, on November 25, 1976,1 started quoting an article published in the Quebec City newspaper Le Soleil on March 25, 1976, which article was written by a citizen of the Sherbrooke area, Mr. Gaston Begin; he described the disadvantages in the fluctuations in the cost of interest which he described as being a parasite. That article is so well written that I feel it is well worth quoting:
"Those financiers are represented by the chartered banks and ably camouflaged by the Bank of Canada which makes only pocket money at the rate of 8 per cent a year on the monetary mass of the country while the others make the rest, namely 92 per cent. With their multipliers, with a stroke of the pen, they cash in on the wealth of the nation and collect unfair interest on it. They take over our wealth and become our masters; they are the tyrants from whom we must ask permission to breathe.
A country must not buy money, it must create it itself, and without being forced to do so. That is the supreme right of the state; otherwise a country cannot be administered. Its economy becomes distorted, turned upside down, damaged, even tainted, as ours is today.
February 3, 1977

Nothing will change if we do not have the courage to force our governments' hand so that they revamp this impostor of a monetary system which directly causes miseries, perpetual indebtedness, inflation, high cost of living and laxity."
I think it is quite in order to deal with the whole flaws of the present banking system, since the object of Bill C-1001 is to create a bank. This is clearly indicated in clause 1, and 1 quote:
1. There is hereby incorporated a corporation under the name Continental Bank of Canada, in English, and the name Banque Continentale du Canada, in French, hereinafter called the "Bank", consisting of such persons as are from time to time shareholders of the Bank.
In short, just another bank.
For all those who seem sceptical when we refer to the role of banks in the creation of money, here is a quotation from a book by Paul Samuelson, winner of the Economics Award of the Royal Bank of Sweden. I have this book here, if anyone has doubt, a book published in memory of Alfred Nobel.
This new edition of the translation is based on the fifth edition of the book reviewed and supplemented by the author, third printing, 1966. On pages 277-278 under the title: Can banks create money? the author has the following to say to explain the basic banking system:
The banking system as a whole can act as no single bank: it can develop its investments and loans to the extent where they reach a multiple of the total resources orginally available to the system. However each small bank in doing so lends only a part of its deposits.
We therefore reply in the affirmative to the question asked at the beginning of this section. Yes, the banking system and the American public jointly create about $5 in bank deposits for each dollar withdrawn from circulation and delivered to the banks.
Is this clear enough? Yet that book can be found in nearly all universities and all collections of the work of Samuelson. I had the opportunity to meet students at the La Pocatiere community college and they told me that they had those books, but that they had not noted the important points that we can discover when we read the books.
Samuelson then explains in three tables how deposits are created.
Table 26 A: Initial situation of the mother bank;
Table 26 B: Untenable situation for a small isolated bank;
Table 26 C: Final situation of the mother bank.
On page 284, the same author says the following:
Through these same processes, the banking system finally creates desposits for a total amount equal to five times that of the additional initial coverage.
This is what we, Social Crediters, talk about regularly and what we try to force government representatives to admit, that we cannot continue to live in a system of perpetual debt when we have federal-provincial conferences to try to discover who will have the right to collect the most taxes from the taxpayer. There must be an end to this. This is a cause of dispute.
Samuelson also explains in Table 26 H the multiple expansion of deposits throughout the banking system. He adds at the end of the table:
... in each generation, each small bank has "created" new currency so that terminal banking deposits are five times higher than the coverage finally collected from the rest of the economy.
Continental Bank of Canada
The same author also says-and I have taken notes to be quite sure that what I am quoting can be checked anytime by anyone so inclined:
We can obtain the same answer two other ways-by using common sense or elementary algebra.
On the following page, page 285, he adds this:
We can now observe that banks as a whole can achieve a credit expansion which a single bank could not achieve.
In Table 26 I, he gives a synthesis of the final position of all banks together. In the field of banking legislation, we have a number of freshmen who show good dispositions, but in an era of electronics and automation they go on using old rusty machines whose gears do not work any more. That is why our financing machine is falling apart. Those in charge of its operation do not even think of putting some oil where it is needed to prevent the bankruptcy which every unbiased observer says will hit us sooner or later.
We are worried by the list of fraudulent bankruptcies and we do not dare take the necessary measures to put an end to that state of affairs because we are afraid of disturbing the big shots who keep on taking advantage of the system.
Usually, at least, the essential product always comes when you can pay for it. Various organizations have studied the matter of housing, so what are the results? We ask from the government a working man's credit, namely loans for those families who want to buy a house. What does that mean? We have enough room, wood, stones, manpower and technicians to build houses. We lack money. Let us make loans and we will see houses being built. Let us do the same in other fields. Let us give money to the father of a family and we will see that he will find something better than rags or second-hand clothes for his children.
Of course, we will not give heaps of money for products that do not exist, but we simply want to give enough money so that a citizen can buy the goods that will help him meet his needs.
Bankers and politicians now say that there is too much cash in circulation. However very few people say that they have more money than what is necessary for them to meet their needs. This is what we can see everywhere.
So we fail to understand why governments take one portion of the worker's pay because the workers' families really need the whole pay of the father to meet their ordinary needs. If there is too much cash in circulation, the government should take it where it is most abundant, but never where it is lacking. Money is a creation of man! But as soon as a problem concerns money, we are stuck, we bow as before to what is inescapable, just as if it was a question of weather. Nothing can be done against the sun nor the rain. Nevertheless some so-called cultured minds take for granted that nothing can be done against lack of money and inability to pay.
However, money is not a creation of God, but an invention of man. Money was not created at the beginning of the world in a limited and immutable amount, by God's decree or by the forces of nature. Nothing such. Whether money be of metal,

paper or whether it be only credit transfers in bank books, it exists because it was made somewhere by man.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you and also my colleagues. However I would tell you as well as to the hon. member who rose on a point of order that I am now well rested and fit. The other day I was about to conclude my speech, but today I can go on again. Mr. Speaker, I hope you will allow me a few more minutes to end my remarks.
In any case the hon. gentleman who rose on a point of order even said it was interesting. So I go on. When the money supply in a country goes up or down, it is because somebody makes or withdraws some money. Money is coming from people who have the power to make it. That is the first thing we must have in mind if we are to overcome the financial obstacles placed between goods and needs, between the wheat in the field and the table around which hungry people sit.
The second thing we have to learn is that money is the only thing in the world that can be made in required quantity. When Canada declared war in September 1939, the whole country had been short of money for a decade. But overnight there was plenty of money until the end of the war. Money came by millions and billions, as much as was needed. That was so in every country at war. How was that money begotten? Certainly not by opening new gold mines; workers were led to the forces and war equipment plants rather than gold

mines. The money came by a stroke of the pen. It was simply decided it should be there.
Food, clothing, shelter require work. Goods are the result of work. But not money. Money is the result of a mere decision by those who have the right or privilege to so decide. This is a point on which I would like hon. members to think, to try and understand all the difficulties in our system. This system could be amended anyway. When this is realized, one can no longer accept that there be no money when the lack of it is the only reason why goods in stores cannot be had by consumers. When this happens lack of money is a criminal mistake fraught with consequences. Name one government that would decide in wartime to send its soldiers home or shut down its war equipment plants for lack of money. This we did not see in Canada. How come then that the same successive governments accepted to leave hundreds of thousands of individuals and families suffer hunger and illness, lose their houses and farms because they had no money? I for one was a victim of the depression. At the age where everyone looks ahead with some confidence, we were living in a crazy system where we were earning 50 cents a day. Because I could never forgive the system for supporting that, I welcome this opportunity to express my views on the current situation.
A country should not buy money, it should create it. Such is the sovereign right of a government, without it no country can be governed, and the economy becomes thwarted, upside-down and weakened as we see it today. We therefore urge the government to use their right to create all the money needed for trade in an active and prosperous country, or to create credit instead of money. But let that be to society's benefit, let us have social credit instead of bank credit where interest is personal and trade like rather than social. It is simply that, but all that.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the debate at this stage of this particular bill may have a rather dreary resemblance to the debate when a former bill, S-30, came back at the report stage. It is true that Bill S-30, accepted by the other place last session, was modified extensively in committee and met the objections of the majority of the members at the time, and it was only by some belated intervention at the report stage that some assiduous but misguided research assistants prepared a number of amendments merely to engage in a doctrinaire blockade of a bill which had satisfied the members of the House after extensive examination in committee. None of the objections which were made at the report stage had been raised at the committee stage. As a matter of fact, it seemed to be an almost total abdication of any examination on the basis that had been suggested. Of course, this is merely a tactical blockade, and this House should be more than conscious of the effect of such a blockade. The blockade may amuse some people, edify others and satisfy some doctrinaire quirks, but the point is that there are some 12,000 people who own a portion of I AC, many of them-
