speechtext:
That is true of the great majority of them. There may be a few wealthy people among them, but it is strange to inquire about the portfolios of 12,000 shareholders of a company like IAC, which is a large, allCanadian company. Some people who care little have a total disregard for how they trample on other people's property, how they may kick them in the teeth and how they may cause them loss without right of repartition. They are quite prepared to act as long as they see fit, but should they feel hurt themselves you would hear them bleat. If those who want to intercede at this time cite one or two names-as was done in debate this afternoon-of people who have worked and risked a lot, it is primarily because of jealousy because these people are smarter or a little more astute.
The hon. gentleman suggests there might be a character in the shape of a dog's hind leg. Unless one is able to put forward proof of misfeasance or improper practices, I think he should not cast aspersions on others. I would like to see the proceedings of this House broadcast when such statements are made. We would see how fast a libel suit would be slapped on. It is easy to make statements in the confines of this Chamber where there is absolute privilege, but they would not dare to make those statements outside. I find it rather difficult to accept observations like that.
This House has to act responsibly. If there are proper objections to a bill and we have heard them, the bill goes to committee and it is examined as to misfeasance, instead of wild allegations being made which have no substance. We should not be caught up in causing potential damage or financial loss to people who have no recourse. Some members dismiss the fact that they can cause economic loss to others by playing games, but if anyone were to start stepping on their toes we would hear them scream.
I put a lot of blame on the government for the fact that certain objections are being raised to this particular bill at this time. A white paper on banking revisions should have been prepared for reference to the standing committee on finance immediately after the conclusion of the throne speech debate. But we are not going to get a white paper, we are going to get a bill and the second reading debate will be extensive because the government will be committed to a particular course of action. After that there will be reference to the committee, and then public hearings. I forecast that the only amendments to the Bank Act in 1977 will be a one-line amending bill about May or June extending the life of the act for another year.
What about this bill to incorporate the Continental Bank of Canada? Does it face another year of total opposition, and is that opposition justified simply on the doctrinaire grounds that banks should be nationalized? There is no other reason for the opposition to this bill.
This is a Canadian operation and it is going to start with some money. I suppose to members of the New Democratic Party, the fact that it makes money makes it a reprehensible operation. To them the only things that are good are loser,
Continental Bank of Canada
state-operated ventures. They all become losers unless they have an absolute monopoly. I think members of that party should examine their stand and the interests that other people legitimately have. It is totally wrong to blockade this bill all through this session. Undoubtedly, if this practice continues it will take another year before the bill can go through. The Bank Act is not going to come forward, and there will be no opportunity to incorporate a bank by letters patent which would eliminate the private bill.
This House has to be responsible to the public interest, Mr. Speaker. Over the years I have seen some shocking examples of abuse of parliamentary privilege and parliamentary practice. People who have absolutely no right of redress have suffered grievous loss. I think those losses should lie in the souls and minds of the people who caused the excessive delays. The case can be argued, and it is then up to us to incorporate the body. We do not guarantee it will operate at a profit.
I dare say members of the New Democratic Party were quite happy to see the Unity Bank go through. It has had some difficulty in its operations, but others have gone through recently that seem to be operating very well and which are likely to be successful. They are like any new business except that the stakes are higher. At the present time, foreign financial interests can operate freely in this country-the suitcase bankers. Foreign banking interests are allowed to incorporate subsidiary institutions, not called banks but carrying out many banking functions, without supervision. This is because there are people who think that some Canadian operations are too big. By trying to get a squirrel with an elephant gun they miss the squirrel but get the much bigger game. I urge hon. members to let this bill go forward to the next stage. Surely the people who are putting forward this proposal are entitled to justice and fair play from this House. That is all I ask.
I urge hon. members not to delay unduly passage of this bill. Some may have legitimate remarks to make. I made plenty of suggestions with regard to the bill last year and was able to obtain many changes, as I saw fit, on behalf of my party, and those changes were accepted by the committee. We are considering a large Canadian company. The result of their proposal would be foreign-owned interests coming in and taking an ever bigger share of our

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I refer the hon. member for Edmonton West to an article in the Financial Post of April 3, 1976?

It was written by Beatrice Riddell and Stephen Duncan. The headline reads, "Stall of IAC Conversion to a Bank Raises Larger Issues ." The article reads in part:

Barring an unexpected change of heart by the 16-member NDP caucus, the IAC Ltd. proposal to convert to a chartered bank appears stopped in its tracks- for the time being at least.
I shall quote what I consider as the main parts of the article. I hope the hon. member for Edmonton West is listening. The paragraph I am about to quote is headed, "Conversion vs Creation." It reads:

The issue, as I said, is one of conversion as opposed to the creation. That question can only be debated fully by members of this House, and of the finance committee, when they see the proposed Bank Act amendments. That, I suggest, is what the two learned authors of the article say.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONVERT IAC INTO CHARTERED BANK
speechtext: Who are they, and what are their interests?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO CONVERT IAC INTO CHARTERED BANK
speechtext:
They are Beatrice Riddell and Stephen Duncan, writers for the Financial Post. I do not know them but have read what they have written in the Financial Post. I am sure that they have both knowledge and experience of this matter.
The article goes on to say:
Ever since the Porter royal commission on finance reported in 1964, it has generally been considered acceptable, and even desirable, for existing near-banks to become banks if they want to do so. But, in fact, this is the first such request.
I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton West remembers the Porter commission report of 1964, and the questions which were raised at that time concerning the conversion of nearbanks to banks. Well, here is a large institution attempting to convert itself into a bank. We say, properly, I think, that before this conversion takes place we should see the new bank act and the standards which are to apply under that new act.
The authors of the article go on to say this:
Obviously, a bank sponsored by an organization of IAC's size, reputation and financial expertise provides much greater potential competition for the existing big banks than one starting from scratch.
"If anyone is entitled to a new banking charter, IAC with its proven management and strong Canadian flavor (96 per cent owned by 13,000 Canadian shareholders) certainly is," a senior Canadian banker says.
Before the Finance Committee on Bill S-30 there appeared the Inspector General of Banks, C. L. Read. He set forth a principle which we should look at very closely. He said that in order to put the banks in a proper perspective we should have more competition. That is the thrust of his statement. That is what C. L, Read, the Inspector General of Banks, told the Senate Banking Committee when it convened in November to hear an application from IAC of Toronto to form the Conti-
February 3, 1977

nental Bank of Canada. He said government policy favours the chartering of new banks to provide competition for the 11 existing banks. If I thought there was real competition among the 11 existing banks with regard to interest rates, I would more than welcome the instrusion by IAC into the banking field. However, one need only look at the interest rates with regard to personal loans, mortgage interest, and rates to companies to realize that there is no competition whatsoever. There may be a little bit of competition with regard to acquiring business and services, but one could not for a moment say that there is any competition with regard to interest rates.
An article in the December issue of Maclean's is entitled "Let There Be Banks-A Little Something For The Rich". After setting forth the principle by C. L. Read, the Inspector General, the writer, Terrence Belford, sets forth the background of the persons who conduct the IAC operation. He says, and I quote:
Take IAC's Continental Bank. Among its 16-man board of directors, thirteen sit on the boards of other banks or trust companies. They are: J. S. Land, Royal Trust Co.; Ronald Cliff, National Trust Co.; Frank Covert, Royal Bank; John Dewar, Toronto-Dominion Bank; Conrad Harrington, Royal Trust Co.; David Kinnear, Bank of Montreal; Louis Lapointe, Toronto-Dominion Bank; Keith MacDonald, Canada Permanent Trust Co.; Paul Pare, Royal Bank; Charles Rathgeb, Royal Bank; Renault St.-Laurent, Banque Canadienne Nationale; James Thackray, Bank of Montreal; and Dennis Yorath, Montreal Trust Co.
With an array of directors like that who sit on the IAC and also on other banks, one draws the immediate inference that competition would remain the same as it is today among the other 11 chartered banks. I would think the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) would see that that is a reasonable inference on the basis of the facts that have been presented by this writer and myself. If you have the IAC with 13 directors who have interlocking directorships with other banks, you cannot reasonably expect competition in the banking field.
Terrence Belford in the article in Maclean's goes on to say, and I quote:
IAC's major shareholder, with a 19 per cent interest, is Carena-Bancorp Inc., controlled by Peter and Edward Bronfman, who incidentally are also principal shareholders in the company sponsoring the Commercial and Industrial Bank. Their partner in Carena-Bancorp, which owns the Montreal Forum and Canadi-ens hockey team, is Jacque Courtois, a vice-president of the Bank of Nova Scotia. The Bank of Nova Scotia itself also participates in Carena through its holdings in Placements Rondelles Inc. Yet another IAC shareholder is Royal Trust. Both the Bronfmans and the trust company will transfer their shareholdings to the new bank.
On the evidence of the article by Terrence Belford, we come back to the original proposition by the Inspector General that the incorporation of new banks will be for the purpose of providing more competition. We find that the directors of IAC have interlocking directorships with other banks. We also find that IAC's major shareholder has many other corporations which are directly related to banks. Therefore the inference is reasonable that there will be little or no competition.
Mr. Belford goes on to say:
This galaxy of corporate talent has managed to convince the Senate banking committee to exempt the IAC bank from many regulations governing similar ventures. For example, the Senate says the Bronfmans can keep their 19 per cent
Continental Bank of Canada
shareholding for two years in spite of the fact all other bank shareholders are limited to a maximum 10 per cent interest.
That is a concession which is worthy of note and worthy of examination. The hon. member for Parkdale said that appears to be discrimination. I quite agree with him.
Mr. Belford went on to say:
The IAC bank bill will allow the company to keep its two insurance subsidiaries for at least two years:-
Again the inference can be drawn that this is a discrimination in favour of IAC against other banks.
-other banks are specifically banned from the insurance business. The bank will also be allowed to keep its current board of directors for ten years even though the Bank Act says directors cannot sit on both bank and trust company boards. IAC has Five such directors including its president, J. S. Land.
On the basis of the evidence by Terrence Belford, we should examine thoroughly and exhaustively the reasons why IAC want to incorporate under Bill C-1001. The reasons are quite obvious. They want to continue their operation with exemptions and preferences that other banks do not now enjoy.
The hon. member for Edmonton West says that there are 12,000 or 13,000 shareholders who may be suffering certain losses as a result of the holding up of this bill. There are 23 million people in Canada. Their interests far exceed the 13,000 shareholders represented by IAC. They do so in light of the favours that IAC would obtain by its conversion from a finance company to a bank.
This is the first attempt by any finance company or near bank to move to a bank. All other applications have been started from scratch. Therefore it behooves all of us to study in depth this problem of conversion versus creation.
When I consider the array of directors, when I consider the type of shareholder, when I read about the exemptions which would need to be made with regard to the finance act, I come to the conclusion that in fairness to all Canadians, not merely to 13,000 shareholders, there is a duty incumbent upon all members of parliament to delay this bill until a new Bank Act has been presented. When we know what the amendments are to be, and when these matters have been fully debated in the House and in the Finance Committee, we shall be in a position to deal with applications from insurance companies and nearbanks in a spirit of fairness, knowing what is contained in the new legislation.
This, in summary, is why we in the NDP oppose Bill C-1001. We have no axe to grind with the hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Reid) who brought this measure forward as a private member's bill. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock, clause 21 was being considered. The hon. member for Nickel Belt had the floor.
On clause 21.

Mr. Chairman, when we broke off at five o'clock for private members' hour I think I was commenting on the great coalition which seems to take place between the two old line parties in this House when we come to deal with such things as changes to the Income Tax Act. I am always very impressed by the way in which the official opposition stops opposing and suddenly becomes supportive of the government when it comes to income tax changes affecting those in the upper income brackets.
As my colleague from Sault Ste. Marie has quite correctly pointed out, we have no quarrel in principle with this particular clause which seeks to increase child care deductions.
We all have families.

Yes, we all have families and know what it costs to raise children in this country today. I myself have five and can attest to what it costs to raise children. So as I say, we have no quarrel with this clause in principle. But we submit
February 3, 1977

the government must be prepared to make some meaningful changes in the structure of the income tax system so it becomes a tool for redistributing wealth. The government is superimposing the kind of change outlined in this clause upon a structure which is badly distorted and as a result, people who earn a lot of money can take advantage of such changes to get richer, while the spread between the incomes of those at the top end of the scale and those at the bottom becomes greater.
The minister has made all sorts of points about the number of people who have taken advantage of child care deductions and so on. But this is not the point that we have been trying to make, Mr. Chairman. The question is: how much is that in actual cash to a family? The National Council of Welfare- one has to assume this council knows something about low income families and income distribution, and one has to assume it has expertise in this field for which, I think, members of the House will be prepared to give it the benefit of the doubt-has shown how the tax saving from the deduction is substantially more beneficial to the wealthy than to the low income groups. The National Welfare Council has pointed out that at the $10,000 level such a $1,000 deduction would be worth $210, while at the $50,000 and plus income level it is worth $410. Here is the kind of distortion we were talking about, that the increase in child care deductions for the upper income bracket would be worth to them twice the amount that a person making $10,000 would have.
Last Monday the Minister of Finance claimed that the quarter of a million Canadians who claim the child care allowance stand to benefit from the increase, but he failed to say that some benefit more than others, and the ones who tend to benefit more are the ones who are already enjoying a greater benefit from society in terms of wages. I think the minister misses the point we have made that in effect this kind of amendment maintains the constant inequality and keeps the spread, and even widens the spread between the upper income groups and the lower income groups.
Not only does this bill deliberately improve the tax position of the middle and upper income earners, it does absolutely nothing to plug the existing loopholes which really turn the ability-to-pay principle upside down. This is a period of time when even societies like ours are concerned about plugging loopholes or at least narrowing the gap between the top and the bottom income levels.
What are all these amendments doing? They are doing nothing to change the fact that in 1974 deletions from the accounts of the income tax revenue that could not be collected because the taxpayers were no longer resident in Canada amounted to $850,000, owed by 161 taxpayers. What attempts has the government made to collect those taxes? In this situation the tax dollars have gone down the drain and the rest of us will have to pick up the slack in that area.
Does the bill do anything to change the fact that in 1974 252 persons who made over $50,000 that year paid no tax at all, and that 17 of them had incomes of over $200,000? Does it
Income Tax Act
do anything to collect these taxes? I want to know that because it is rather important.
Another question that one should ask oneself is whether this bill does anything to change the fact that professionals who want to avoid taxes set up dummy companies, since small businesses pay taxes at a lower rate when compared with marginal rates in the personal income tax system. What are we doing to plug that loophole to make sure that that segment of society pays its fair share of the taxes? These are the kinds of questions that we would like to ask. Do we not see some of those changes being brought here as well as an increase in child care allowances? Does the bill do anything to change the fact that interest costs on money borrowed for the purpose of investing in something that may ultimately earn income for the taxpayer is deductible in the year in which the interest expense is incurred? Does it do anything to plug that loophole?
We are prepared to say that if you are plugging those loopholes with amendments in the bill, then of course what you are doing with respect to increased child care expenses has relevance. Indeed, when the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie repeated what the Prime Minister had promised in 1971 in respect of closing the gap between those who have and those who have not, we realize that that philosophy seems to have changed because as recently as January 26 the Prime Minister said the following at a Press conference:
It is not part of the Liberal philosophy to equalize everybody towards the middle; to make sure that the top quintile and the lower quintile are equal, or even, for that matter, very close. It is part of the Liberal philosophy to make sure that the poor in this society get richer. If the rich get richer too, we really do not take offence to that.
I do not mind if the rich get richer, but surely they should not be getting richer with the connivance of the income tax structure which permits all sorts of loopholes. Surely that is not fair. Surely any person who has a sense of justice would never subscribe to that theory. Suddenly it is 1977 and the Prime Minister has changed his tune.
Some of the rather interesting distortions in the income tax structure are rather disturbing. It should be very disturbing to members on the government side to realize that the just society has been in effect for eight years. Certainly we cannot see any justice with respect to the way the changes to the Income Tax Act have come to the House during that time.
I want to point out that we on this side of the House do not oppose the whole concept of increased child care cost exemptions. However, in this debate we want to focus attention on the distortions in the income tax structure. It seems to me that the Income Tax Act certainly provides loopholes which not only benefit the rich but are a deliberate tax policy of the Liberal government. This helps to explain the fact that in 1971 taxpayers in the $25,000 and over income group, where ownership of stocks, bonds, mortgages and business interests are concentrated, paid only 13 per cent of the federal personal income tax, while those taxpayers earning less than $10,000 paid 51 per cent. To know that it is a premeditated, deliberate attempt on the part of the government to help the rich get richer we only have to look at the remark which I mentioned
80008 - 3314

Income Tax Act
earlier made by the Prime Minister at his press conference on January 26.
But we have seen other amendments go through the House. We have seen changes with respect to the surtax. That occurred when the anti-inflation program was established. They were supposed to go in tandem. Here we see one coming off and the other staying in. I suppose this is what the minister would term the way ahead.
There is no question that when we look at the bill and we see the elimination of the surtax, we see changes with respect to the registered retirement savings plan, and when we see the write-off on personal income tax of moneys put into exploration, we become very concerned about these kinds of proposals with respect to child care expenses moving up because in effect they will not really help the lower income persons in terms of cash. We have no hesitation at this particular point in saying that this clause is going to be inequitable when taken together with the other changes which are envisaged in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I rise in this debate because at an earlier stage last week when we used some figures to suggest that the overwhelming percentage of the savings made by these various income tax provisions which the minister is proposing would go to people in the upper income bracket, the minister argued against the points put forward by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, by myself and others, using figures with regard to registered retirement savings plans. He was supported by the hon. member for Edmonton West. They argued that a very large majority of the people taking advantage of these plans were people in the lower income brackets, people earning up to $15,000 a year.
Ten thousand.
The hon. member for Edmonton West interjects that they are people earning under $10,000.
Taxable income.

Taxable income, and technically he is correct, but we have had some calculations made from the information provided by the Department of National Revenue and Statistics Canada, and while the hon. member is technically correct, if we look at where the savings actually go, it becomes very obvious that the real savings go to the people who earn over $10,000, and particularly to those who earn over $15,000.
I think it would be useful to put the precise facts on the record. The argument advanced by the minister and by the hon. member for Edmonton West is the usual argument we hear, not just from politicians from the Liberal and Conservative parties but also from people who write financial columns in newspapers, business editors and so forth. We have a typical example of this in an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 20, 1976 written by Ronald Anderson, and which reads as follows in part:
... the retirement savings plans encourage people to save for their retirement, the home ownership assistance plan helps and encourages people to provide their

own living accommodation, and the interest and dividend exemption encourages Canadians to build a modest investment portfolio.
As I say, this is the typical view of middle and upper income people because they look upon themselves as being typical of all Canadians, and of course nothing could be further from the truth. These plans encourage thrift, supposedly, on the part of those who can afford to save, and in these days that is not very many people. These gimmicks are supposed to foster savings, but they only foster savings if people have extra money to save. In 1974 there was a total tax benefit of $513 million from the registered retirement savings plan, and the figures show that most of that went to the affluent. Last week the minister argued that RRSP's were not benefiting the wealthy at the expense of everyone else because in 1974, the last year for which we have figures, nearly 940,000 people had RRSP deductions. What the minister did not tell us was where the benefits accruing from these deductions went.
We have had an opportunity to look at statistics which show that just under 5 per cent of the people in the $20,000 and over category got over 57 per cent of the tax savings in 1974 from RRSP deductions. I will put the figures on the record, and I would be happy if the minister could show us that we are wrong. People with a taxable income of under $5,000, 38.4 percent of all the people who took advantage of this provision in the income tax law, had an average saving in taxes of $1.02 for the year. The people who had taxable incomes of between $5,000 and $10,000 per year-and they made up 31.5 per cent of the people who took advantage of this provision-had an average saving for the year of $9.81. The people who earned between $10,000 and $15,000 taxable income-they made up 18.7 per cent of those who took advantage of this provision- saved an average of $38.43.
Now we come to the big winners, those people who had taxable incomes of between $15,000 and $20,000 a year. They made up only 6.8 per cent of all the people who took advantage of this provision, and they saved an average of $125.01. People with taxable incomes of over $20,000 made up 4.6 per cent of those who filed under this plan, and they saved $551.88. That is the kind of rough justice the Minister of Finance believes in, $1.02 saving for those who have taxable incomes of under $5,000, and $551.88 for those who had taxable incomes of over $20,000. That is the just society of the Trudeau Liberal government.
Let us look at the registered pension plan, which the minister said was a better illustration of equity than any other. Registered pension plans were supposed to benefit the ordinary working person as opposed to those more affluent. The savings are divided up in the same way, although the result is not quite so extreme.
Of those who took advantage of this plan 38.4 per cent had taxable incomes of under $5,000 a year. Their average saving was $1.85. Of those who took advantage of registered pension plans 31.5 per cent had incomes of between $5,000 and $10,000, and their average saving was $21.29. Of the people who took advantage of the registered pension plan 18.7 per cent had incomes of between $10,000 and $15,000, and their
February 3, 1977

average saving was $73.26. However, when we come to those people earning between $15,000 and $20,000 taxable income, they made up only 6.8 per cent of those filing under the registered pension plan, and they saved $135.76. Those people who earned $20,000 taxable income, and who took advantage of this plan had an average saving of $225.50, and they made up 4.6 per cent of those filing. In other words, under this plan those who were able to make use of it and who earned under $5,000 saved $1.85. People earning $20,000 taxable income saved $225.50. That is another example of what the minister considers just.
If you combine these two sets of figures and look at the total retirement picture you find that those with low income and no other resources get virtually no help. They get the old age pension, but then so do the wealthy. Supposedly income tax takes away from the wealthy-except that the minister permits them all kinds of exemptions.
The affluent and powerful who have other sources of income, and who do not need to worry about retirement, receive generous benefits from the government. We have calculated this as follows. The group with under $5,000 taxable income per year have an average saving of $2.88; between $5,000 and $10,000, $31.10; $10,000 to $15,000, $11.68; $15,000 to $20,000, $260.77; and over $20,000, $777.38. The same applies to the Registered Home Ownership Plan about which the minister spoke so proudly this afternoon.
I did not mention it this afternoon.

If the minister did not mention it this afternoon then I will not deal with it. There is one other thing which distorts the whole tax structure and which again is a bonanza to those in the upper income brackets, and that is the indexing of income tax. We consider this to be the biggest boondoggle of all. It is an idea that the Liberal government stole from the official opposition several years ago. It has been touted as a plan which benefits everyone because all save the same as a result of inflation, and therefore if income tax is indexed everyone receives equal benefit. If you look at the actual figures, however, you see that as usual under a Liberal government those at the top benefit much more than those at the bottom.
The tax rate at the bottom is much higher than it needs to be. If you give money away to everybody, particularly to the wealthy, then you have to find the money to meet expenses. To pay for the services you have to take the money back from everybody, and take more from those at the bottom.
Using figures supplied by the Department of Finance we looked at the savings for a taxpayer with two children under 16 for the years 1976 and 1977. The group with a taxable income of $5,000 a year will pay $46 less tax; $10,000, $284 less; $15,000, $413 less; $20,000, $621 less; $30,000, $884 less; and $50,000, $1,259 less.
Income Tax Act
These savings are for what the Department of Finance called a typical taxpayer at various income levels. In fact even these figures do not tell the whole story because people in the upper income bracket do not make all their money from wages and salaries. They often have income from capital gains which escape taxation and are not taken into account. No account is taken of other potential deductions that I spoke of earlier such as child care, RRSP, RHOP, interest income deduction, and so on.
I think we have demonstrated quite conclusively from the statistics issued by the government that our system of taxation is geared to give the greatest benefit to those who already have. This is why we have the situation which some of us have spoken about for a number of years where, despite all the plans for social security, despite the fact that we now have hospitalization insurance, medical insurance, family allowances, despite all these federal and provincial programs, rather than the gap between rich and poor being narrowed, in the last 25 years it has widened.
One of my colleagues quoted figures on this earlier today, and I want to close by putting them on the record myself. In 1951 the bottom 20 per cent of income earners, as a percentage of the total income, received 4.4 per cent of the gross national product. The figures we have show that in 1975 this had dropped to 3.9 per cent. On the other hand, the percentage of the total income received by the top one fifth of the income earners in 1951 was 42.8 per cent of the GNP; in 1975 this group received 42.4 per cent. We believe it should be the objective of a modern industrialized society to ensure that no one lives in real need. The gap between those at the bottom of the income scale and those at the top should be narrowed. This government has not done that and this bill will not do it. It is for that reason that we oppose the bill, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, we listened this afternoon to arguments that were supposed to pertain to clause 21 of the bill which deals with deductions for child care, but although I listened carefully they seemed to relate to other matters. I suppose there is not a clause in the bill which does not relate to the Income Tax Act and I think the New Democratic Party have at least grasped that fact. I should like to answer some of their arguments.
The new act passed in 1971 was piloted through this House by one who now sits in the Federal Court. Taxing laws are complicated, and certainly not all accountants or lawyers understand them. Mr. Chairman, I have just returned from the Canadian Bar Association's mid-winter meeting, and it is the opinion of the association that no act is as difficult to understand as that act to which I just referred, which was passed by parliament. In saying this I am not criticizing the government, because no matter which party is in power, Liberal, Conservative, or even NDP, the drafting of tax laws is an expert's job. And, Mr. Chairman, hon. members listened this afternoon and for three quarters of an hour this evening to the biggest drivel you ever heard. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, would you trust any

Income Tax Act
one of those people to my left-and I say this to the press as well, even though only one press man out of 70 is in the gallery-would you trust any one of them to do your tax return? Those people are terribly ignorant about tax matters.
I suppose you are an expert?
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
There is ignorance personified.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Chairman, considering from where that remark has come, I will not even ask for withdrawal. The hon. member in his rhetorical question asked if any people would trust us to do their income tax. The answer, of course, is that it depends on whether you are rich or poor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is entering the debate. He and other members of his party have had a chance to speak without interruption; I think he ought to let the hon. member for Calgary North continue.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that interruption. When talking about child care deductions hon. members on my left covered the whole scope of income tax. Mr. Chairman, every day I sit close to the leader of the NDP; although I am not in my seat at present, this debate being in committee of the whole. Mr. Chairman, every day the leader of the NDP rises to criticize the government with regard to unemployment. Really, what the hon. member's party says- and I should like the Liberals to listen-is this: if a person makes a profit or earns a high salary, unless you tax him right down to the poverty level there is something wrong with the country.
I say people must have the right to a profit, since profits lead to investment. You should be able to make a little money, because then you can invest in the industrial development of the nation. But the NDP wants to bring us all down to one level. Really, when they talk about 30 per cent unemployment here, 20 per cent there, and 10 per cent in Quebec, the NDP are saying this: tax everybody to death; give the money to various organizations or spend it on phony programs, and then blame the government for unemployment.
Hear, hear!

Really, that is what we are talking about. Mr. Chairman, I have been here for a long time. We have witnessed an NDP filibuster. But then, they are merely trying to maintain their votes, the votes of people with a certain level of income. They are trying to show that they have done their job on behalf of those people.
Oh, oh!

I am glad you are yelling and shouting. That party is trying to hang on to its votes, trying to show that

it is doing its job. Let me deal with what they talked about earlier.
How do you know what we said? You were not here this afternoon.
We told him.

Those hon. members discussed the child care expenses, and in so doing covered the whole field of income tax. That brings me to my point concerning the Income Tax Appeal Board. When you, as a taxpayer, raise a matter coming under section 21, or any other section before the appeal board, if you win your appeal the Crown will not disclose what cards it has up its sleeve. When I speak of the Crown I am not speaking of the minister; my remarks in this regard are not meant to criticize the government.
Hear, hear!
The same old gang.

Hon. members on my left should consider what is happening in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; they can laugh if they like, but we are not talking specifically about governments; I am talking about the tax act. If the taxpayer wins his appeal before the appeal board, the Crown will not disclose its cards. If it does not like the board's decision, it can take the matter to the Federal Court. Mr. Chairman, in Federal Court you are not allowed to say that you won your case before the Income Tax Appeal Board. You start from scratch. Therefore, you might as well scratch out the Income Tax Appeal Board, because it does not work to the advantage of the taxpayer. No matter whether he has raised any question coming under section 21, 22 or 23. I hope the minister and his officials will take my remarks into consideration. I say, if you are going to have an Income Tax Appeal Board, give that board some powers.
This afternoon the NDP tried to make representations on behalf of the little taxpayer.
I suppose you are one.

Hon. members on my left can laugh and shout, but they are not really concerned about the rich or the poor. They are concerned about the fact that they now have the best jobs they will ever have in their lives.
Oh, oh!

I raise the point concerning the Tax Appeal Board because I happen to know something about it. I know that if you take your case to the Income Tax Appeal Board and win it, you might as well forget it, and I will tell you why. The Crown is not worried if you are rich or poor, but it is worried in case the appeal board decision sets a precedent which could affect many people, be it one million, 100,000, 10,000, or any number you can think of. The fact that you have won your case before the appeal board has no weight at all at the Federal Court level. I therefore say to the minister, if
February 3, 1977

there is to be an Income Tax Appeal Board which is empowered to render decisions, surely one should be able to appeal the board's decisions to the Federal Court in the same way as one can appeal in the appellate court of a province a decision handed down in the superior court.
I did not realize the situation was quite as bad as I have painted it until I listened last week to a Canada Bar Association lecture. As things now stand, the appeal board is a nullity because it does not matter if you win or lose your case. If the Crown thinks you have a good case, it will not disclose its cards before the appeal board, but will wait for the case to be heard in Federal Court. I ask the minister to look into this question. Perhaps some of the problems which even NDP members raised in committee might be solved more cheaply at the lower level, because if you must go to the Federal Court, you have to hire lawyers, and the whole process is much more expensive. Who can afford to go there? These are important matters.
I now want to move on to something else. We have been talking about the whole realm of income tax. This is an important clause to many people, but there is something even more important. All across this country people are struggling to get a house. Some may have a little savings that they can put into a second house, a small farm on the prairies or small piece of land in Ontario or Quebec. One of the most destructive things with regard to investment has been the capital gains tax. I will state why.
A person may have invested his savings in a small piece of property. At age 65 he will be going on pension and may want to sell that property. The valuation was set on January 1, 1972. I am not talking about rich people. I am talking about those to my left who preach their drivel. They are the ones who wanted the capital gains tax for every farmer in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta.
Flear, hear!
I will bet that when my friends to my left go to Saskatchewan they do not tell the public they were the ones who were in favour of it.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I realize it poses quite a difficulty for Your Honour to hear me over the noise that is going on. Nevertheless, I believe I have a legitimate point of order. As much as I admire and respect the hon. member for Calgary North I am sure he would not want to leave a misleading impression in this House. If he will go back to the debates on capital gains to which he referred, erroneously I am afraid but I am sure it was unintentional, he will find that while we were in favour of full taxation of capital gains, we made it very clear during the entire time that the family farm was to be exempt. We are for motherhood just as he is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let us say that was a point of clarification.
Income Tax Act
It is time we had a debate like this. The only reason they get up is because I am telling them the truth. They cannot stand to hear the truth.
Hear, hear!

The fact is that if you go through the committee records and the records of this House you will see that the NDP were for capital gains taxes. If it had not been for this party, we would not have had the amendments to protect the average man and the family farm.
Let me get back to what I was talking about, the little person. Whenever I do that, the NDP members get irritated. They try to leave the impression that they are like God and the angels, the only people to look after little people.
The average income earner may buy a small house or little piece of property. Immediately he sells it he must prove the evaluation to the department. These people who are elected to the NDP like bureaucracy. Therefore you have to hire an appraiser and an accountant and get other expertise to prove the valuation, or else the tax department will gouge you. That is where the NDP should be directing their attention, instead of peddling that drivel they have peddled all night. Socialism led to unemployment and the destruction of the United Kingdom. It would destroy Canada if this government ever followed their example.
Hear, hear!
Conservatism destroyed it.
I can answer that very easily. The hon. member says conservatism destroyed Canada. We have not been in power that much in Canada since John A. Macdonald left the scene, to destroy anything.
Hear, hear!
However, that party was in power in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia and we know of the destruction there. It is very difficult with a debate which I hope I am leading tonight-
Hear, hear!
Maybe this is the only night I will lead the Tories. At least I am bringing some life into the Chamber. It has been dead all day. The NDP filibustered all afternoon on clause 21.
What are you doing?
This is the first time I have spoken on this bill, but it won't be the last.
Hear, hear!

Under the general administration of the Income Tax Act, you can have an assessment in 1972, one in 1974, one in 1975 and one in 1976. It can all be approved by the department. All of a sudden, the person who wants to sell

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
comes to my office to his member of parliament and says that the bureaucracy wants to reassess him because they do not agree with clause 21, even though that person has had approval for four years. I want to make a very serious suggestion either with regard to this clause or the next. We need a group of men and women in the department who will meet with the ordinary taxpayer and say to him, "If you have done A, B and C, that will be it and it will not change in three or four years."
The ordinary taxpayer does not have the accountants of the CPR, Canada Permanent or the Royal Bank. He has to rely on himself or possibly one accountant. What we need in the department is a small group to sit down with the taxpayers and tell them, "If you make this move, this will be your tax position, this is the amount of tax you will pay and it will not be changed in three or four years because of someone reinterpreting the act."
I have had a lot of experience with the department in Calgary. I have worked with top accountants in reference to these matters. There is the finest group of men and women in the public service. Unfortunately, many times a problem affects many taxpayers. Therefore it cannot be settled in Calgary, or even in Regina, or Winnipeg. It must be done in the east. Instructions come from the east because if a precedent is established with regard to one taxpayer, it could change the whole tax picture and, of course, the flow of revenue.
I will be open with the minister. I think he has looked at the picture in a tougher and more realistic way than his predecessor. He has been, in the circumstances, with inflation and unemployment, a pretty able and reasonable Minister of Finance.
Hear, hear!
You are preaching for a call. Next week you will be supporting John Turner.

That's fine. You can yell or shout. You can do that from the stomach or from other parts of your anatomy but not your mouth, if you have a brain. What I would like to say is this: please get together a group from every part of the Department of National Revenue, whether it is Calgary, Vancouver, or right across the board, and have a group the average taxpayer can go to and say, "If I make this move will it be accepted today or four years from today?" That will win the NDP a few votes which have faded ever since I have been here. That is a recommendation which I make tonight-and I know something about tax law. I have listened to members of the NDP-
You were not here!

Yes, I was here. I have listened to you people. I will back my attendance against you, you little-you know what I mean-any time. But take these three recommendations I have made. It doesn't matter what is put into the act, because if it is interpreted in a certain way by the department the taxpayer doesn't stand a chance.

I ask the minister to take a look at what the capital gains tax is doing to the little person. Let us have some way of assessing the effect of the capital gains tax without needing to consult a lawyer, an accountant, and an appraiser. Arrange things in such a way that if a taxpayer has a problem he can go to the department and get a decision made, a decision which will not be reversed in four years time, upsetting his whole economic applecart. That is what I am asking, and these are the problems the taxpayer is worried about more than the nonsense I have listened to today. Those people-and I will say this about the NDP-want to take all the money away from anybody who makes more than $10,000, except themselves.
We don't!
Oh yes, parliamentarians do. It is the best job you will ever have, young man.
You devil!
I am a devil because I am telling you the truth. The devil has to tell the truth sometimes.
I got elected.

I know. That was an accident and it will never happen again. Those people over there preach these things. They want to take all the money from all the little people, from business, from the corporations so that there is no investment, and when people are out of work they will say to the taxpayers I have mentioned, "Aren't you terrible? You have caused unemployment." But that party's economic principles are such as to ensure built-in unemployment.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, first of all, I want to congratulate the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. He made what was certainly the most sensible speech we have heard this evening. It is indeed good to hear a man who doesn't hesitate to express his mind.
I do not have a long contribution to make to this debate because I was not aware what it was about until I heard the speech made by my hon. friend from Calgary North. But since this seems to be a wide-ranging debate and since it does not seem altogether necessary to keep to the point, I should like to put one or two questions to the minister.
My hon. friend was most eloquent when he spoke about the need for the bureaucrats and the rest to look after the small taxpayer. I have a question about a large taxpayer. I think the way in which his case is being treated is a public disgrace and I want to know when it will be proceeded with and when justice will be done. I refer to the case of John C. Doyle, the owner of Canadian Javelin Limited and the man who controls it or who owns 18.2 per cent of the shares.

Order!
February 3, 1977
Mr. Chairman, if we had the TV cameras here tonight there would be no fear of the NDP ever getting into power.
Hear, hear!

Their strong point is pretending that only they have decent perceptions-that they are the only decent people in Canada, the only ones who care. We are sick and tired of their hypocrisy. They pretend, the NDP, the party of newly decent perceptions, that they and they only have the welfare of the public at heart. That is the line they hand out all across Canada. Well, it doesn't fool me. There is not a member of the NDP who has the public interest more at heart than I do, and their blatherskiting about how they are for the small man, the little man, is enough to make anyone throw up.
Hear, hear!

We have had to sit here listening to their blather hour after hour, and now they will have to sit and listen to ours.
The point I am making has nothing to do with the small taxpayer. It has to do with a large taxpayer, a fugitive from justice, the man who has had control over Canadian Javelin Limited for the last 20 years and who has taken money from that company in every way, shape and form, and who has diddled the shareholders of that company year after year, and the law is apparently powerless to do anything about it.
There are 18,000 unregistered and some 12,000 registered shareholders of Canadian Javelin Limited. The company's shares are no longer listed in most of the registries and do not trade. The gentleman in question now resides in Costa Rica and Panama, because if he comes to Canada he faces 406 charges under certain sections of the Criminal Code, and two for criminal fraud in Newfoundland. But he still has control of the company. And he still owes the Canadian government in excess of $4 million under a judgment delivered in the Exchequer Court five years ago by Mr. Justice Hugh Gibson. That judgment was appealed by Mr. Doyle. Five years later, Mr. Chairman, the appeal has still not been heard and the amount is still outstanding.
I would like the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue to tell me what is being done about the large taxpayer-
Order!
-and why this matter has not been brought before the appeal court long hence. Will it, in fact, be brought before the appeal court?
Order!
What do you mean, "Order"? There has been no order in these matters. I should like the minister to tell us what has happened in this case.

Order!
Income Tax Act

If somebody has a point of order to raise, I am willing to sit down and listen. This is not order, it is disorder when a situation of this kind confronts us in the courts and nothing is being done about it. I want that matter attended to and I shall be asking other questions about it.
While we are considering the Income Tax Act I should like the minister to get me some information as to the effect on provincial revenue of his arbitrary and unilateral amendment to the act several years ago when he indexed income taxes.
The minister opposite in the government of Canada collects income tax not only for the government of Canada. He also collects the federal corporation tax for at least eight provinces, perhaps nine. He also collects the provincial corporation tax. In his budget of two years ago, I think it was-I do not have all my notes here tonight so some inexactitude might be forgiven me-he indexed income tax without consultation with the provinces, without asking the provinces what they thought about that. He brought down his budget and in his budget indexed personal income tax.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is all well and good. If the federal government can afford to index personal income tax-and heaven knows, they can do so because they have all of the tax sources in Canada, direct and indirect-then that is fine. But there are provinces which cannot afford any loss of revenue. Because it is a more efficient system and it suits the Government of Canada better to have certain provincial taxes collected by the federal government, the federal government collects personal income tax and corporation tax for seven or eight provinces. To do so these taxes must be uniform in their application or the minister cannot very well collect taxes for the provinces.
The hon. gentleman therefore made a change which applied not only to federal personal income tax but to provincial tax as well. I should like to know, as a result of this arbitrary action taken without consultation, what it costs the various provinces of Canada to have the income tax collected. I understand that it is costing the provincial government of Newfoundland this year some $30 million when you take into consideration not just the tax collected directly but its effect on tax equalization. The province of Newfoundland alone has lost $30 million of its revenue. This is money that the Minister of Finance took away from the province without so much as a by your leave, and without ever offering to replace the revenue he took away from those provinces whose income tax he collected.
That is one reason-there are many others-why we have the present state of federal-provincial relations in Canada today. It is the reason why the provinces are calling out for more decentralization and for a change in the distribution of powers. It is not the constitution which is all that much out but the way that it is administered. Nothing is more irritating and aggravating to provincial governments than to have the federal government make a change like this without even consulting them and agreeing to compensate them for such a change, so I would be interested to see those figures if the hon. gentleman
2704

Income Tax Act
would get them. He may not be able to get the figures showing what the loss of tax equalization might be, but if he can tell me what it costs the various provinces, including the province of Newfoundland, by way of lost tax revenue from the change that he made, I would appreciate it.
I believe these are the only two points that I want to put forward tonight, unless some hon. gentleman down in the corner says something that might irritate or aggravate me, in which case I will be on my feet again. We are not worrying about the NDP up here in this corner because we know they are nothing to worry about. They are a necessary irritant, like a burr under the saddle. It does us some good to have them around, because when there are a few of them around you realize what you would suffer if they ever formed the government. As I have said, and NPD government would comprise a cabinet of about 30 incipient Otto Langs; at least that is the way I look at it. They know what is good for us, and by golly we do what is good for us or they would know the reason why. It would be user-pay multiplied about 100,000 times if those gentlemen ever got into power.

Mr. Chairman, I think hon. members would want me to irritate the hon. member for St. John's West just a little bit to have him keep going. I have known him in some different capacities over the years and I never cease to find him an entertaining man when he is on his feet.
With regard to his two points concerning Mr. Doyle, very happily the Minister of Finance does not have custody of tax administration; my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, has that. Indeed, if the matter has gone to litigation and is before, I guess, the Federal Court of Appeal at this point, it would be a responsibility shared with my colleague, the Minister of Justice. I cannot, therefore, answer this evening the status of that particular suit, but I would be quite prepared to make inquiries and if this is not a matter of confidence on behalf of the taxpayer-and if it has come to the point of litigation-then I would be glad to let him know.
On the question of indexing, it is quite true that both federal and provincial revenues have been affected by the decision of this government several years ago to introduce indexing of personal income tax. We calculate that as of January 1, 1977, with the indexing which occurred then, on an annual basis for 1977 about $1,250 million of federal and provincial income tax will be left in the hands of individual taxpayers which, but for the indexing, would have been collected under our taxation system.
That was Stanfield's policy.

As the hon. member for Calgary North points out, that was the policy of the member of parliament for Halifax. Indeed, we have been castigated over the years by the hon. gentleman's colleagues for having adopted that particular policy. As I say, Mr. Chairman, he is always a refreshing speaker, but not the least when he is doing things,

as Frank Sinatra would say, his way, rather than the way of his party generally.
It is true that revenue has passed out of the government's hands and back to the taxpayer. If you talk about decentralization, that is almost the best kind of decentralization to have if you can possibly have it-leave the money in the hands of the people and not take it away by tax.
If the provincial governments, like the federal government, needed additional revenue they are not powerless in this regard; they could have changed the rate and recovered it. But the fact of the matter is that, despite all the protestations at federal-provincial meetings, there has been pretty general acceptance of that and of the decision that was made.

Mr. Chairman, during the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary North and the hon. member for St. John's West, I felt very strongly that I really had to rise on point of order after point of order, but I restrained myself knowing that the Chair would at some point recognize me. I think it is important, particularly to the hon. member for St. John's West who seems to be very concerned about whether we in the NDP think he is decent, that he should know that I have spoken to every single one of my colleagues here and we all agree that he is decent. We all agree that all the Conservatives are decent. As a matter of fact, we never listen to what the Liberals say to us about the Conservatives. So we say he is decent and he is not to worry about it. We think you are all decent fellows.
We have been speaking for quite a long time on this clause in the bill, and I have to tell you frankly, Mr. Chairman, that we were getting to the point where we were having a little difficulty. After all, our voices were starting to give out, and so we appreciate the kind of assistance that we have been getting. We have been sitting here day after day arguing this bill, trying to get the Conservatives to state a position. While I do not like closure and we have all spoken against closure, the fact that closure has been brought in has seemed to prompt some members to rise and speak.
I want to say a couple of other things, particularly to the hon. member for Calgary North. I want him to know that I am not against rich people-some of my best friends are rich people. We are for everybody. I do not talk about it too often in public but I must admit that we do not have anything against rich people; the only thing we are concerned about is that the rich people do not get any richer than they are-that is all. I also want to say that it was not very nice of the hon. member to have made the remarks he made about the election of my colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt, having been an accident.
He said himself he got lucky.

The first time he was elected it might have been an accident-these things can happen to anybody-but the second time it was wilful mischief on the part of the people of Nickel Belt. They elected him deliberately and they sent
February 3, 1977

him here so that you could take the measure of this man. You must admit that you know he is around. Whether you may agree or disagree with some of the remarks that my friend may sometimes bring to the attention of the House, I am sure nobody would say that he hides his light under a bushel. He makes sure that the brilliant light that emanates from him is distributed evenly toward everyone.
I think there is something else that should be said. In putting forward the arguments we have on behalf of people in Canada who are not quite as rich as other people, we may not have been as successful as we had hoped in moving the hard heart of the Minister of Finance. After all, one of the qualifications for being Minister of Finance, even if you have a nice, soft heart, the way the minister used to have before he became Minister of Finance, is to be like that. Once you become Minister of Finance, there is a kind of needle that they have in that department which they jab into you which hardens the arteries, the heart, and occasionally the head. But I am grateful for one thing.
Perhaps we have not moved the Minister of Finance, but as people who believe in making love, not war, we are just delighted to see the Liberals and the Conservatives falling in love with each other all over again. It is really very touching to see this kind of affection taking place. During the day we hear them calling each other names, but we know it is a lovers' spat, we know it is not for real. They are calling the other side all kinds of terrible things. They are saying the Liberals are guilty of all kinds of scandals and that they are depriving people of civil liberties, but this is just like a family. You know deep down that when it is something important such as taxes which affect the rich man's pocket book, they are in love again.
Hear, hear!
These are lovers' spats; they are for the neighbours.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You should know, Maxi.

The hon. member for Calgary North said that this is the best job we will ever have in our lives. He may be right. I bet some of us have had pretty rotten jobs in our lives. I do not know what jobs he has had in his life, but most of our guys have had pretty rotten jobs, just like the people in Canada have. That silver spoon was not placed in our mouths at birth. There may be better jobs than this, and I am sure there are worse jobs. I do not crab about the job. The food is not bad and the pay is not bad but, as my mother-in-law says, it is not a very steady job.
You yourselves voted against an increase in pay. That has always amazed me.

You amaze very easily.
My friend, the hon. member for Calgary North, spoke about the accident of the election of the hon. member for Nickel Belt. I can assure him that it is not as easy even for New Democrats to be elected in Ontario as it is for a Tory to be
Income Tax Act
elected in Alberta. You do not even have to show up to be elected in Alberta.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You try it, Maxi.
If I were a Tory I would be a shoo-in in Alberta, but not being a Tory-

I would not want the hon. member to be historically wrong. When I first ran, there was one member from Alberta who was a Conservative-the rest were all wise men; they were the Social Crediters. I must tell you that I was the first member ever to be elected from Bow River. I would also remind the hon. member-and the former premier of Saskatchewan would know that-that I left home with a grade eight education and took all my high school grades by correspondence. If that is a silver spoon, I can tell him I do not understand silver, but I did find out one thing, that once they had a CCF government in Saskatchewan, they found out what silver was like.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I suggest the hon. member get back to the debate on clause 21 of the bill.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Now we can head back to a somewhat more serious discussion.
How did you like that commercial?
I wish we had television in the House.

I am glad to learn that the hon. member for Calgary North was not born with a silver spoon in his mouth- it might have been a brass spoon, but not a silver one. Nevertheless, I want to say one thing to him. The remarks we are making are not of a personal nature. We know he is a fine, upstanding Conservative. As to how the Conservatives replaced the Social Crediters, the thing happened so that almost nobody noticed. They went out, changed their hats, and came back and said, "Yesterday I was a Social Crediter and today I am a Conservative".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Chairman, this clause, I understand, will eliminate the principal business test for a 100 per cent writeoff of Canadian exploration expenses for taxation purposes. I understand that previously someone in business could write off 100 per cent while investors whose principal business was not natural resource oriented could only write off about 30 per cent. As well, government incentives such as drilling incentives or provincial aids to encourage increased exploration, are not required to be handed out with the exploration expenses before calculating exploration development deductions.
I should like to try to put this clause into the context of what has been happening in the resource industry in order to try to assess whether the amendment before us will have the desired effect of spurring exploration for oil and energy. I therefore look at the largest oil company in Canada and its record of exploration, and I have some serious reservations about the effect of the clause.
Through advertisements on television we find that Canada's largest oil company, Imperial Oil, needs more revenue to explore for new oil. According to the oil industry we are rapidly running short of this precious resource. But is that really true? Does the oil industry need more incentives through the tax system to encourage it to explore? I should like to look at the history of Imperial to argue just the opposite.
In 1972, the last year before the international oil price increase, and in 1975, we find the production levels of this company were virtually identical. There was a dramatic change in the earnings of the company between 1972 and 1975 and we should try to find out how this affected exploration. In 1975 their revenue was $4,047 million, an increase of 98 per cent over the 1972 revenue of $2,104 million. In 1975, the profit after taxes was $250 million, an increase of 65.6 per cent over 1972. A very important category if we are talking

February 3, 1977
Income Tax Act
about exploration budgets is the cash flow which was $464 million in 1975, an increase of 53.6 per cent over 1972.
What happened to the company's oil exploration budget when it earned this record income in 1975? Remember, Imperial has been advertising about the big, tough, expensive job of exploring for oil, and telling how it needs more revenue and less taxes if new energy sources are to be found. What was the exploration expenditures in 1975 after these record earnings? It was $74 million, the exact same amount as it spent in 1972. It has been making the argument on television and in other media that it needs more money through price increases to the consumer for oil and gas. That does not hold water- should I say oil?
Gas.

In the light of the record of earnings of this company and its exploration budget, what has it been doing with the profits? Certainly it has not been putting them into exploring for new oil. It has been diverting money into the Syncrude project in Alberta because of the tax incentives built in through special legislation passed in this House a few years ago. That legislation exempts Imperial from federal corporation tax on its provincial royalty payments, and under the system the company can write off $4 for every $3 invested in Syncrude.
In light of that kind of record of financing of exploration, and in light of the other tax incentives in existing legislation which urge Imperial to divert funds from exploration into projects like Syncrude, I wonder what this amendment will do to enhance exploration in this country. It is an attempt to get further funds from other investors put into energy exploration, but when the companies themselves have other priorities that the income tax system seems to dictate to them, I do not think this clause will have the desired effect.
In light of past experience what guarantee is there that this tax amendment will promote energy exploration? 1 think Canadians will seriously ask this question. Companies claim they do not have enough incentive to explore from the recent increases in the price of the wellhead barrel of oil but companies again have produced record profits for 1976. If we break down the wellhead price of a barrel of crude oil as of January 1, 1977, $9.75, we find that the cost of producing that barrel of crude oil is 68 cents; provincial royalties in Alberta, for example, account for $3.90; federal income tax, $1.54, but the profit on that barrel of oil is $3.63, or 40 per cent of the total price. I submit that there are enough existing revenues to promote exploration for oil for the benefit of Canadian consumers.
The multinational oil companies which control 90 per cent of this country's oil industry at the moment are not serious about developing new energy reserves. They are playing the scarcity game, predicting shortages so that consumers and the government will be panicked into accepting ever higher prices. One should consider the situation in the United States today.

There natural gas is in short supply, mainly because of a poorly designed distribution system, and because, as some think, there has been collusion on the part of energy companies to keep energy supplies at low levels. This has been done because the companies want to press for changes to oil and gas legislation now before the Congress of the United States.
One must ask, considering recent events in Canada, can the oil and gas companies be trusted? Only a few years ago they were predicting that we had enough oil available to last us for many decades. Of course it was in their interest to say that because they wanted to export 50 per cent of Canada's oil production. When the world price of oil went up and the Canadian price remained comparatively low, it was to the advantage of oil companies to change their song, to change their predictions. Suddenly we learned that estimates of reserves had been revised downward. The many billions of barrels of oil which we were previously told we possessed suddenly disappeared, and the oil companies said that unless they could charge the world price for oil in Canada they would not be able to explore for new oil reserves.
I have tried to show what has happened in the case of Canada's largest oil company, Imperial Oil. Although that company has made record profits and enjoyed a tremendous increase in cash flow, it has not carried out exploration, exploration which would reassure Canadians that more oil will be available. I therefore submit that clause 24 of Bill C-22 will probably be ineffective in the long run, and that the government in the past was manipulated by the oil industry. Having examined clause 24, it appears to me that once more the government is bowing to demands of the industry and has designed tax legislation which will unduly benefit the oil industry.
For those reasons I submit that we ought to look carefully at clause 24 and ask the minister and his officials to tell us what the effects of this clause will be. If the minister could guarantee that if we were to pass the bill, including clause 24, we should see an increased exploration for oil, and that we shall establish an ongoing monitoring agency to ensure that exploration will take place, I might be persuaded that clause 24 is of value. But, Mr. Chairman, when I consider the record of the oil industry, I have some reservations. I think of the Syncrude deal the minister was blackmailed into signing that fateful day in Winnipeg when he was accompanied by the then president of the treasury board and the Minister of Supply and Services. I just shudder at the thought that the present Minister of Finance, who was then the minister of energy, mines and resources, has proposed legislation of this sort.
Canadians have given far too great a tax advantage to multinational oil companies. The government is providing further tax incentives, and not only to energy companies which have enjoyed the advantage of a 100 per cent write-off. Any business, energy-related or not, will now be able to qualify for this 100 per cent write-off.

No wonder the Tories like the Liberals.
February 3, 1977

Mr. Chairman, that makes one wonder about the government's priorities. Members of my party have examined various other clauses of this bill which are designed to give a greater dollar advantage in terms of income tax to upper income Canadians. It is obvious that clause 24 is designed to fit into that pattern as well.
Our income tax system is supposedly progressive. The percentage of income payable as tax ranges from a low level for low income earners to a somewhat higher level for high income Canadians. However, as I said this afternoon, and as other colleagues said this evening, the concept of progressivity based on ability to pay is subverted by the kinds of deductions for which the bill provides, because the percentage of income payable in tax at upper income levels is reduced.
I doubt if the exploration expense write-off provided in clause 24 will have the desired effect. I say this, bearing the history of the oil industry in mind, and because this tax law has been designed in the context of unfairness and inequity.
