subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADMINISTRATION-POSSIBILITY OF EXISTENCE OF GUIDELINES GOVERNING ACCEPTANCE BY DEPARTMENTS OF FREE ADVERTISING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention this evening arises as a result of the question 1 raised on December 15, 1976, with respect to a matter which had originally been addressed by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) to the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais). The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain, I may add, was subsequently elevated to the great office of Whip on the government side.
The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain had asked the Postmaster General if the Post Office had accepted a freebee from Time magazine, a freebee with respect to Post Office advertising in that particular publication. When answering, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he did not understand my question, that he did not know what a freebee was. I found this difficult to understand because in a number of instances during the past few years the term "freebee" has been used in the course of debate in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister, much to my amazement, was not able to understand in a very simple question asked of him during the course of the question period what a freebee was in terms of political activity. The Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) appears to be very agitated and
Adjournment Debate
excited when I mention these things. I simply want to say that it is a term that is not in the Oxford dictionary, but indeed is in the dictionary of the cathetral of here and now in which we address ourselves in the House of Commons.
I say to the parliamentary secretary, who apparently is here tonight to answer this question, that a freebee can be defined on a number of occasions by actual performance of members of the Treasury Bench. Freebe is a very understandable term. Quite frankly, it involves a situation where the government and members of the government accept, without payment, a kind of reward that might in fact influence the activities or decisions of government. I do not suggest for a moment that is the case. However, we who are involved in the governmental process should be very concerned that we do not do anything that might in fact be interpreted by the public as being something that might influence governmental decisions.
When we talk about freebees, we may be concerning ourselves with the perception that people have of what government is doing and what government might in fact be inclined to do in the area of discretionary decision.
My question to the Prime Minister at the time simply asked whether there was anything in the government guidelines that might determine not only whether it would be appropriate but proper from the point of view of acceptance on the part of government of free advertising in the communications and publications industry. The time that I raised my question was after a question raised by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain with regard to an answer by the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) to the effect that the Post Office had accepted a freebee or overt gesture by Time magazine to try to improve the service of the Post Office by means of an advertisement placed in that magazine.
Although the question of influence peddling may not be legally provable in this case, certainly the practice of accepting free advertising from companies whose activities are directly affected by government legislation, such as in the case of Time magazine, is questionable. It suggests a serious lack of judgment on the part of the department and the government. It also bears a direct relationship to the use by ministers and members of parliament of aircraft owned and offered by private companies or foreign countries.
I mentioned at that time, when the Prime Minister evinced some surprise at the term freebees, a few examples he might consider, for instance, the use of private jets belonging to liquor companies, the use of jets belonging to a particular lobby group, the Canadian Bankers' Association, by the minister of consumer affairs at a time when the question of consumers affairs legislation was before the House. That association is involved in making representations to the government regarding amendments to the Bank Act, and other important legislation-

GRAIN-USE OF ELEVATOR SPACE FOR DURUM OR RED SPRING WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 13, 1976, as reported at page 1919 of Hansard, I asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board the following question:
In view of the storage space available in Canadian government elevators in western Canada, for example, some four to five million bushels in Moose Jaw, and in view of the fact that utilization of this space for Durum or Red Spring wheat would inject some needed funds into the western economy, would the minister undertake to instruct the Wheat Board to take immediate steps to utilize this space to the advantage of the producers and businessmen in the communities?
To which the minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker. I would not give that instruction to the Wheat Board. The Wheat Board is fully aware of the existence of that space and also of the extra cost involved in using it and the advantage of using it. I am sure they weigh these factors and come to conclusions which are in the best interests of farmers.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), to whom I put a supplementary question, had this to say:
I am sure the hon. member knows that these elevators cannot be used to the extent we would like them to be used unless the Canadian Wheat Board instructs that the grain be delivered there. Full utilization has to be with the full co-operation of the Wheat Board and the trade in general.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
In western Canada there are five government elevators. They are located at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton and Lethbridge. These elevators have a total capacity of some 17,100,000 bushels. According to Grain Statistics Weekly, which is a weekly publication of the Canada Grain Commission, for the week ending January 19, 1977, there are presently some 6,634,000 bushels of grain in storage in those government elevators. If you deduct that figure from the
17.100.000	bushel capacity, there is storage space for roughly
10.500.000	bushels in these five elevators. Of that 10,500,000 bushels of available storage space, approximately one half, or
5.300.000	bushels, is available in the terminal elevator at Moose Jaw.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is no quota, for example, on Durum except for those chosen few who were fortunate enough to receive a special quota for the two types of Durum, Macoun and Wakooma. I am concerned as to why the Wheat Board cannot set up a special permit to allow the other people who have Durum in storage to deliver and utilize those
10.500.000	bushels of available space in these elevators, or, on the other hand, to use the space to store Red Spring wheat and thus put additional money into the hands of the producer and into the economy of western Canada.
There has been a suggestion that it is too costly to utilize these government elevators, but it seems to me that it is costly to allow these elevators to lie idle or at least not to use them to maximum capacity. It is also costly to have boats sitting in Vancouver harbour for several weeks on end waiting for grain to be loaded. Over the year end, I understand there were some seven to eight boats in the harbour at Vancouver, and while I was unable to get the figures for demurrage, a Canadian Press report indicated that a Chinese boat in the harbour was costing the western farmer some $10,000 a day in demurrage. If my math is correct, that $10,000 would pay for the storage of one million bushels of grain for one month in one of these government elevators.
The Moose Jaw terminal has a capacity of 5,500,000 bushels and has a throughput of anywhere from 25 million to 30 million bushels a year. Yet according to the annual report of the Canada Grain Commission for 1975-75, there were only 34 million bushels put through the five government elevators in western Canada, and the historical average is only 20 million bushels.
The Moose Jaw elevator can dry, clean and place the grain to export standards, and it can load a hopper train of 100 cars a day. Those 100 cars will carry 330,000 bushels of grain- approximately a third of a million bushels, and the average ship carries a million bushels. So in three days the elevator at Moose Jaw-that is one of five-could send out sufficient grain to fill one boat and the railway can carry that from Edmonton, Moose Jaw, or Calgary to the west coast in two days, so there would be no need to have these vessels sitting in the harbour at Vancouver where we are paying demurrage. If anyone cares to look at Hansard of January 24 at page 2284,

in response to written question No. 687 by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn), they will find that in the period of one year from October, 1975 to October, 1976, the prairie farmer paid over $4 million in demurrage charges on the west coast at Vancouver, and approximately $1 million at east coast ports.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GRAIN-USE OF ELEVATOR SPACE FOR DURUM OR RED SPRING WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government elevators to which my friend, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), has referred in his question this evening follow an established policy to work closely with producers, with grain companies and, of course, with the Canadian Wheat Board to make these very important facilities in western Canada available in a manner that will maximize Canada's grain movement both for export and for domestic purposes.
In day to day operations, space is made available in each of the elevators to accommodate Canadian Wheat Board requirements as they arise. This has its greatest application particularly for high moisture grain. Other such applications relate to special accumulations and storage of specific grades of grain, especially during periods of unprecedented demand when bunching of vessels occurs in Vancouver.
As well, currently about half the space at Lethbridge is leased out to local feeders and processors, thereby fulfilling a useful purpose in this heavy feeding area.
As my friend pointed out this evening, Canadian government elevators do not buy grain themselves. That is, of course, the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board and the grain trade.
In deciding whether or not to utilize Canadian government elevators at any given time, the Canadian Wheat Board has to evaluate a number of factors including the cost of assembling grain in the terminals by producers using their own trucks, by custom trucking or by rail movement; as well as the over-all space available in the primary elevator system and the advantages to the rail shipment program which the Wheat Board has established at any moment in time.
Until this week no Durum quota had been established by the Canadian Wheat Board in the current crop year. However, there has been a heavy Durum movement since December through Vancouver and it is anticipated that this will continue at least until the end of March. This has allowed the Canadian Wheat Board to establish effective February 1, a Durum quota of 4.46 bushels per acre, or, as some would want to know, 300 kilograms per hectare. This will enable producers to deliver into the licensed elevator system and provide an injection of funds into the western economy.
There is currently under way a heavy shipping program for Red Spring wheat through the west coast which will continue at least until the end of May. This will be augmented by an eastern movement through Thunder Bay upon opening of Seaway navigation.
Adjournment Debate
In view of this, Mr. Speaker, the Wheat Board at this stage of the crop year does not see the need to utilize the government interior terminal elevators. Of course, as circumstances change later on in the year, the situation could be reviewed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ed Lumley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-NEWFOUNDLAND- GOVERNMENT ACTION IN VIEW OF CLOSING OF LINERBOARD MILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to expand on the response which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) gave on November 17, 1976, to the question from the hon. member for Humber-St.
George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) concerning Labrador Linerboard Limited.
DREE is aware of the difficulties which the provincial government is facing in respect of that provincial Crown corporation. However, the minister has not been approached by the province in respect of the recently reported closure of the linerboard mill at Stephenville.
The provincial government recently announced the establishment of a study committee and a reorganization of the corporation's management with the objective of examining and recommending an alternative course of action.
As the hon. member should be well aware, our department is primarily concerned with effecting improvements to the basic economic structures of areas such as the Atlantic region and identifying and pursuing development opportunities of a long range nature. There are other mechanisms designed to alleviate the economic and social hardships which arise from the short term unemployment resulting from difficulties experienced by a particular company. I must say that it is my understanding that the Labrador Linerboard Mill at Stephenville was closed recently for an indefinite period, due to high production and raw material costs, as well as poor world market conditions for linerboard. I have also seen reports that mills producing linerboard in western Canada have closed recently for the same reason.
DREE has played an active role jointly with the provincial government in Newfoundland in attempting to develop the province's forest industry. In April, 1974, we signed the Forestry Subsidiary Agreement with the objective of expanding and diversifying the forest industry in Newfoundland and Labrador through a series of projects on forest management, access road construction, harvesting and utilization, and other forest improvements. That agreement initially provided for an expenditure of $34 million on such activities. It was amended in January of 1975 to provide an additional $17.7 million, so that federal participation in that agreement represents a financial commitment of almost $48 million. The amendment, incidentally, was intended to increase further the sustainable level of utilization of forest resources on the island of Newfoundland through the use of mechanized logging equipment, the establishment of logging camps, and the construction of an additional 400 miles of forest access roads.
The amendment to the agreement also made provision for joint initiative with the provincial department of forestry and agriculture to improve the efficiency of the wood harvesting operations of Labrador Linerboard Limited.
Needless to say, we very much sympathize with the position of the Newfoundland government which is faced with continuing deficits in the operation of the mill. However, I must emphasize that the operation of the Crown corporation is the responsibility of the provincial government and does not directly involve our department.
